Input: What is the belief of atheists regarding the explanation of everything through science? Is there a possibility of something beyond explanation according to atheists? Science is by far the best tool we humans have for understanding objective issues. If we can't understand an objective issue through science, we basically can't understand it at all. I think a lot of people have a misconception of science being stuffy or overly formal, and not understanding just how flexible it can be. Generally speaking, science is a method of gathering evidence, trying to come up with explanations for that evidence, and then trying to think of further ways to evaluate those explanations to be sure that they really are accurate. Throw in a bunch of lessons learned on how to avoid common pitfalls and cognitive biases, and you've got 'science'. And while the stereotype of science is white lab coats and beakers, all the various fields of science are far, far broader than that. Subjects like anthropology, history, religious studies, and linguistics all fall under the social sciences. ABOVE: Some examples of the social sciences, since most people are already more familiar with the physical sciences SOURCE: Branches of Sciences - Physical, Earth & Life Sciences | Leverage Edu Even many pseudosciences try to incorporate the trappings of legitimate science. When you look at ghost hunters, for example, they are trying to compile evidence around these issues, with things like electronic voice phenomenon, EMF meters, photography, eyewitness accounts, dowsing rods, Ouija boards, etc. What separates a pseudoscience like ghost hunting from legitimate science isn't the lip service to evidence based reasoning, but in the rigor of testing these explanations and properly accounting for those pitfalls and cognitive biases that can trip us up. But, if ghost hunting ever will become reliable and credible, it will be by addressing those shortcomings, more rigorously following the standards of legitimate science, and presenting evidence and explanations that are truly convincing. So many so-called 'other ways of knowing' may sometimes have value in subjective issues, moral lessons, teaching, or even entertainment, but they're no replacement for science when it comes to evaluating objective issues. Without evidence based reasoning, such methods are worthless at this task. And the more they do incorporate evidence based reasoning, the more they come into the fold of science, anyway. Of course, that's not to say that science can actually explain every objective issue. For example, as of right now, we don't know what caused the Big Bang, and may not ever know. But importantly, no other human endeavor besides science can address the question any better. For example, you may feel your religion provides an explanation, but your neighbor who practices a different religion might feel that their religion provides a different explanation, while yet another neighbor with yet another religion believes an altogether different explanation. How do you determine which religious explanation is right without resorting to evidence? Whoever claims to feel it the strongest? So like I said, science is the best tool we have for addressing objective issues. And when such questions are beyond scientific explanation, as they sometimes are, they're beyond any human explanation, at least for now. Yeah, yeah. I know. There are more things in Heaven and Earth, Horatio… But of course, that line was invented by a 16th/17th century playwright, trying to use ghosts as a plot device. It’s easy to diss on skeptics when you’re writing a fictional universe where you can simply make fantasy happen.

Atheists, isn't your Darwinian theory a little far-fetched when you think about it? The theory states that all living things have a common ancestor. An elephant and a mosquito share a common ancestor? Really? When I've talked to people about this, part of the misconception seems to be expecting something like a mosquito evolving into something like an elephant, or vice versa. But that's not the way evolution works. Both mosquitos and elephants are highly evolved, complex creatures. But their common ancestor wasn't anywhere near as complex as either of them. Here's the oldest known bilaterian animal (i.e. the group that includes elephants and mosquitos). This likely isn’t the actual, specific common ancestor, but it would have been fairly similar. SOURCE: Oldest “bilaterian” found: wormlike creature discovered along with its tracks From our modern point of view, that's a pretty simple, worm-like animal (though in its own time, it was one of the more complex creatures yet to evolve). But from that worm-like form, as it's descendants carried on and diversified, each separate lineage was free to 'add on' to that body plan, evolving into more complex forms as time went by. But since they were separate lineages, they couldn't share mutations between them. Each lineage went its own way, so that the types of complexity that evolved in each lineage was different from their cousin lineages. SOURCE: ResearchGate.net - Origin and Evolution of Nervous Systems As far as insects in particular, you can trace their evolutionary history, and see how various traits evolved generation by generation, eventually resulting in the complexity of modern day mosquitos: SOURCE: Fossils, genes and the evolution of animal limbs - Nature Likewise, you can trace the independent evolutionary history of vertebrates, which followed a different path, resulting in a different type of complex body plan: SOURCE: Fossils, genes and the evolution of animal limbs - Nature In fact, you can do this for the whole tree of life. The organisms we see today are the tips of the branches. The tips didn't evolve into the other tips. Instead, you have to trace the branches back in time to find the common ancestors that the branches evolved from. SOURCE: Researchgate.net - Informational Ecological and System Approaches for Complete Genome Analysis So, that’s how mosquitos and elephants evolved from a common ancestors. That ancient ancestor wasn’t yet very mosquito-like nor very elephant-like. It was really much more worm-like. It’s only as time went on, and each of those lineages went their separate ways, that one particular lineage evolved into mosquitos, while a different lineage evolved into elephants. As an aside, all the normal caveats go here. Most Christians and other religious folks accept evolution, so this isn’t an atheist vs. religious issue. And most folks only use ‘Darwinian’ in a more historical context, and specifically in reference to natural selection, to contrast with other ideas on evolution (like Lamarckian use and disuses). The modern day theory is the Modern Synthesis, which includes many more concepts and principles than Darwin ever knew about.

Do they still teach the myth about Columbus being the first European to reach the Americas in US schools? They don't teach that myth, but some schools might still teach other myths. Back when I was in school in the '80s and '90s, they already taught us about the Vikings reaching Vinland before Columbus. But there was still too much hero worship and mythology around Columbus, which has persisted at least through my own daughter's education just a few years ago (she's now in grad school). Many folks still get the impression that Columbus proved the world was round, rather than the truth that so many of his contemporaries were skeptical of the success of his voyage because they knew the true size of the Earth, and that his ships wouldn't have enough supplies to get all the way to Asia. He really lucked out in 'discovering' an unknown continent. There's also not much coverage about how cruel he was. I mean, he went beyond the 'normal' bad behaviors of European colonialists towards the native Americans, and was actually arrested by fellow Spaniards and taken back to Spain in shackles (Lost document reveals Columbus as tyrant of the Caribbean). Still, Columbus's voyages really were a watershed moment in history. The Viking settlements in Vinland were short lived and didn't have much impact on European or American history. To the extent that other Europeans even knew about it, it didn't seem like much more than another Iceland or Greenland just a little further west. It was only after Columbus's voyages that Europeans realized that there were two entire continents that they'd never known about before, kicking off the transatlantic relations now known as the Columbian exchange. Whether you consider that good, bad, or some combination, it certainly made a huge impact on world history. So Columbus's voyages rightly receive more attention than the Viking settlements in Vinland, even if Columbus wasn't the first European to reach the Americas.

Is it considered rude to be served on paper plates and plastic utensils at a dinner party? It depends on the formality of the party and the number of guests. But even then, there are other options besides paper plates. If it's hot dogs and hamburgers from the grill, paper plates are fine. If it's prime rib, roasted potatoes, and grilled asparagus, you'll probably want to serve those on something nicer. If it's a small enough dinner party to where you own enough plates to cover it, go with real plates with real silverware. But if the party gets bigger than that, then it's just a practical matter that you have to do something else. We do this every Christmas and Thanksgiving with my wife's family. She has a pretty big extended family, so these are meals for several dozen people. But we still don't go with paper plates. We try to compromise with 'nice' disposable dinnerware. Something like this, which is actually plastic plates, plastic utensils, and a plastic wine glass: ABOVE SOURCE: Sam's Club But some other family events get hosted by family members not quite as concerned about 'formality'. So then it might be paper plates and regular plastic utensils. And, well, taking the time and spending the money to provide a meal for the whole family is generous enough. Rude would be turning up your nose at that meal because the dinnerware wasn't fancy enough. Basically, if you're doing the hosting yourself, try to use dinnerware that matches the formality of the meal, even if it's disposable. If you're attending an event that somebody else is hosting, appreciate the generosity even if it is paper plates.

Are atheists truly correct if everything has to have a creator? The Earth can't come out of nothingness. It had to be created by something. If everything has to have a creator, then who created the creator? Some higher level creator? And who created that higher level creator? An even higher level creator above that one? Does this chain keep going and going for infinity? That's not mere snark. That's the exact same existential angst inducing thought process I had when I was still a Christian which left me laying awake in bed plenty of nights. It's not philosophically satisfying to say that a god created everything. You still have to explain why that particular god exists and has the properties it does (as opposed to somebody else's god from some other religion). And, perhaps most importantly, you have to explain how a god makes more sense than other ideas about how the universe got started. Trying to figure out how the universe got started is mind bending with or without invoking a god. But invoking a god doesn't really offer a more satisfying answer than non-religious explanations. If anything, trying to saddle the 'uncaused cause' with personality, feelings, and though processes just seems even more implausible. And to be clear, we have a pretty good idea of the history of the universe from the Big Bang on. But in the spirit of your question, I’m answering about the universe as a whole, since we know more or less how the Earth formed as part of our solar system from a nebula.

I have responded to a fare number of Christian trolls on here as a Christian myself, so this is an honest question. Regardless of which theistic religion, would there be anything that could convince you of the existence of a god(s)? If so, wouldn’t that make you more agnostic that truly atheist? (I believe the wisest amongst us are the agnostics) All knowledge is provisional. Pretty much everything I think I know could be a mistaken belief. For an example, let's take something extreme like the roughly spherical shape of the Earth. In everyday language, I would say that I know that to be a fact. But, I can also imagine scenarios where I might be wrong. These might seem like absurd scenarios, but I can't rule them out entirely. Perhaps I'm living in something like The Truman Show, where I've been misled my entire life merely for the entertainment of some viewing audience, and what I think is the real world is merely a very, very elaborate set. Maybe 'real' society is much more advanced than my simulated society, and I'm living in something like a Star Trek holodeck, with advanced AI generating the bredth and depth of this deception (e.g. why I can google convincing evidence for a spherical planet). If you could produce and show me sufficient evidence along these lines, then you could convince me that the Earth really was flat. But, in everyday conversation, I'm not going to say I'm agnostic over the shape of the Earth because of that. It's the same way with gods. I think they're very, very unlikely, on par with me living in The Truman Show. But, that slim chance still exists, and sufficient evidence could change my mind. But why treat this one question differently from all other knowledge questions? Why use a special word to denote that I might possibly be wrong about the issue of gods, when that same possibility also exists for everything else? No, in common usage (as opposed to some corners of the Internet who try to define the term differently), 'agnostic' means someone who's unsure about the existence of gods, not merely somebody who could be convinced with sufficient evidence. So going by the common usage, 'atheist' really does describe me better, as I really am quite sure that gods don’t exist.

So why are pilots who have been flying for years all saying they know the earth is flat? In any sufficiently large group, you can always find a few cranks and screwballs with odd conspiracy theories. In the U.S., there are something like 600,000 people with pilot licenses, with around 100,000 of those working in commercial aviation (How Many Pilots Are In The US?), not to mention military pilots. If even just one out of a thousand of those pilots believe in a flat earth, that's 600 total pilots, or 100 commercial pilots – certainly enough to throw together in a YouTube video with a long list of 'testimonials'. Now, I'm pretty immersed in aviation myself. My own job is an aerospace engineer. I got my pilot's license back when I was in college, working a couple summers at the airport. I currently live in a town with a lot of influence from our local Air Force base. So, between my job and personal life, I know lots of pilots, aerospace engineers, and even a few air traffic controllers. And I don't personally know any of them who believe in a flat earth. It's the type of thing we joke about from time to time, but not something that anybody takes seriously. I don't know of any polls or studies to put numbers to this, but if you want some perspectives beyond my own, you can check out pages like this reddit thread: Or read this article from AOPA about a pilot's experience flying around the world: In short, there are so many pilots that I'm sure you can find a handful who think the Earth is flat. But these guys certainly aren't representative of the field as a whole.

Some people say Jesus didn’t resurrect but was resuscitated by Joseph of Arimathea, after which he lived secretly in other parts of the world till the age of eighty. If true, why didn’t the apostles know about this and allegedly died as martyrs? I've seen a few of these ideas with a mix of skepticism and credulity, where they're skeptical of the divinity of Jesus and the supernatural aspects of the stories, but they still treat the overall accounting of events as a fairly reliable narrative. Other similar ideas I've heard include Jesus only being in a coma, or disciples secretly stealing the body. But why? If we already think that the gospels are unreliable accounts, then why accept anything in them at face value that needs any more explanation than simply saying it was made up? Now, I don't necessarily mean that all of the stories were intentional lies (though I'm not ruling it out, either). But rather, the gospels weren't written down until decades after the supposed events had taken place, by people who never met Jesus in person and were relying on oral history that had plenty of time to morph and become exaggerated in the retellings. Any stories in the gospels are just as likely (if not more so) to be urban legends or mythologizing than anything based in fact. So, assuming that there was a real Jesus at the core of this legend, and that he was indeed executed by the Roman authorities, how do we explain what happened to his body? More than likely, it was left up on the cross for a while as an example. And whenever it was taken down, it was probably thrown into a mass grave with other executed criminals and political dissidents. Whatever the inspiration for the belief in the resurrection (and I cover some possible scenarios here - Jeff Lewis's answer to What does a Quoran atheist, with a Christian upbringing, think actually happened following Jesus Christ's crucifixion?), there's little reason to trust most of the details in the gospels, and thus little reason to try to think up more rational explanations. There may well never even have been a Joseph of Arimathea in the first place. As far as apostles and/or disciples dying as martyrs, those stories are partly in the same category. The stories in the New Testament of Christian martyrs are themselves of dubious accuracy, so we really don't know just how widespread martyrdom was. And as far as it did happen, well, people believing in urban legends and conspiracy theories is hardly surprising. You can find plenty of modern day examples in just a few minutes on Facebook – even folks so committed to their beliefs that they staged an attempted coup on the U.S. Capitol, and one man who even martyred himself when he lit himself on fire in protest of a criminal trial against former president Donald Trump. People within echo chambers and cults can build themselves up to committing extreme actions that those of us on the outside find shocking and irrational. In short, there's no reason to spend undue effort trying to rationalize all the different details in the gospel stories, when perhaps the most likely explanation of most stories is urban legends and mythologizing that grew over the decades the stories spread as oral history. But just like in the modern day, there were at least some people who did very much believe in those urban legends, probably enough to lose their lives over those beliefs.

👋 Hello. Although I have many reservations about the New Testament, I wonder why so many people put pen to paper about the life of Jesus. What inspired them to write about his life. Surely there is a 'Kernel ' of truth contained within them? I guess there are two shades of meaning to this question. Why did people write about Jesus at all (which I'll cover first). And why did so many people write about him in particular, to the relative exclusion of similar cult leaders at the time (which I'll get to a bit later). Broadly speaking, people were motivated to write about Jesus for the same reasons that they write about anybody. I've discussed a more modern day cult leader here on Quora before, Sathya Sai Baba*. He just died relatively recently in 2011, and you can find a ton of stuff written about him by his followers, from an official biography, to innumerable online essays by rank and file followers. You can even find answers by many of his followers right here on Quora (just type his name into the Quora search bar). Whatever you might think of his own motivations (e.g. were his 'miracles' intentional sleight of hand deception), he struck a chord with people and was able to parlay that into fame and a successful movement in his lifetime. Will Sai Baba's cult survive for centuries like Jesus's did? Who knows? Some sects seem to die out with the death of their leader, while others seem to resonate even afterwards. There are plenty of examples of this persistence, from major religions right down to smaller sects – Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Zoroastrianism, Mormons, Seventh-day Adventists, Rastafarianism, Scientology, etc. I don't think there's really any way of knowing why Jesus's cult became so hugely popular compared to all the other similar cults in that time and place. Heck, history has relegated John the Baptist to basically supporting cast in the Jesus story, despite being a leader of a religious movement in his own right.** There have actually been studies on smaller scale versions of this. Back in 2003, some researchers created a music download website that they could control to run experiments. They tested a specific set of songs across multiple groups. None of the groups could see what songs the other groups had downloaded or how the other groups rated all of the songs. So in each group, there was equal opportunity for any song to go 'viral'. And what they found that was it was probabilistic and random at the same time (stochastic). Some songs tended to end up in the top downloads more often, while other songs tended to remain relegated to the bottom, but the specific songs that became the most popular varied from group to group with no way to definitively predict it ahead of time. It seemed to come down to random chance and extreme sensitivity to initial conditions. Here’s a pop-sci article discussing the study, and the actual research report: So, there probably was something to Jesus's message about loving your neighbor, caring for the poor, and not being judgmental that resonated with people. But why that particular cult ended up becoming a major world religion as opposed to the similar cults is probably down to chance. Had history played out a bit differently, billions of people might now be worshipping John the Baptist, wearing necklaces with dinner platters instead of crucifixes. * That previous answer about Sathya Sai Baba can be found here: ** It’s interested to read Josephus’s mention of John the Baptist, where he describes John the Baptist as an important figure in his own right, not some second fiddle to Jesus like in the Gospels:

Maybe a biology teach in a public school can’t teach the truth about the existence of life. But can she point out the fallacies of evolution without speaking about creationism? Is that unconstitutional? You seem to be a bit confused or misguided. As much as we can be sure about anything, evolution and universal common descent do appear to be the truth about the diversity of life. When you look at polls of actual scientists, the support for evolution is overwhelming. And, hopefully obviously, school science curricula should be based on the expert input of actual scientists. ABOVE SOURCE: For Darwin Day, 6 facts about the evolution debate Now, there are plenty of fallacies around the public understanding of evolution, and these are exactly the types of things teachers should be covering (e.g. Lamarckism, Great Chain of Being, teleology, etc.). I'll admit, I had several of those misconceptions myself before my high school biology class, and that class really did help set me straight by addressing a few of those fallacies head on. But the supposed fallacies that many creationists like to use have been addressed and debunked over and over and over. One of the most comprehensive treatments was done by Mark Isaak back in 2006, addressing several hundred common creationist arguments: If you think you've found a fallacy of evolution that supports creationism rather than clarifying evolutionary biology, check that list or similar resources, first. I'd bet dollars to donuts that you haven't actually found a fallacy at all (especially knowing the history of some of your other questions, and that you've proposed the evolution as eyes as a problem for evolutionary biology). As far as the constitutionality of teaching these creationist falsehoods, I'm not a lawyer, but I certainly can't see how a teacher would be protected from teaching false information to students, even if the teacher themself sincerely believed it. It would be akin to a flat Earther teaching such views in a geography class, or a math teacher teaching that 2+2=5. The teacher would have the constitutional right to believe such things themself, but not the right to mislead students. The school would be perfectly justified in disciplining such a teacher, and firing them if they persisted.

WHEN does the real future of radical improvement like safe flying cars for the masses, holographic movies, massive building structures like seen in Judge Dredd etc actually start? Are we trapped in the present nightmare of potholes, jammed roads etc? I think you might want to consider what travel was like just a century ago before calling the present state a nightmare. I wrote an answer once about travel in the 1800s and early 1900s (Jeff Lewis's answer to Before the industrial revolution when there were no cars or planes how did people travel and how far would they typically go?). A 30 mile trip would have been an all day affair back then. Now I can do that in around half an hour. It took Wilbur Wright a week to travel from Dayton, Ohio to Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. Google tells me I could make that drive in a little over 10 hrs, which is within reason for a single long day. Automobiles and the Interstate Highway System (or equivalent freeways in other countries) make relatively high speed long distance travel accessible to common people. As far as common sci-fi tropes like flying cars and holographic movies, you can't invent something physically impossible. As far as we know, there's no way to create levitating vehicles, except by already understood physics like magnets, which limits your altitude to something like a maglev train, or aerodynamics, which is basically just an aircraft, and we already have those. You're never going to see something like the cars in Blade Runner that just seem to float in midair with no visibile means of propulsion. Of course, there's more than one use of the term, flying car. If you mean an aircraft with folding wings or a folding rotor, people have already built prototypes of those. The big issue is that the compromises make them subpar aircraft and subpar ground transportation – the worst of both worlds. If you mean a dedicated aircraft that doesn't drive on the road, the issue comes down to physics and hover efficiency. Helicopters look the way they do for a reason. And even the new batch of eVTOL aircraft still have a large amount of total area for their lifting devices to have any type of reasonable efficiency. ABOVE: Various eVTOL Concepts – I don't think this is what most people think of when they hear the term 'flying car'. SOURCE: eVTOL is Almost Here: What About Pilot Training? The way holograms are portrayed in movies is somewhere between very, very difficult to impossible. Keep in mind that what we see is light heading towards our eyes coming from specific locations in space. You can't just make light originate from points in space from nothing. You need something to reflect it off of, or some medium that you can make glow at certain points to generate that light. Here's one of the approaches I've seen that comes closest to what people think of as sci-fi holograms, but just imagine the engineering difficulty of scaling this up to something that could generate an entire full color screen, without the particles interfering with each other, and with opacity (instead of just see through 'wireframes'). And other than the gee whiz factor, how useful would it even be? We've already got the ability to make 3D movies, and they only come and go as brief fads. People seem perfectly content with regular movies. And movie makers use that medium to frame shots and show things from specific perspectives. Horror movies would lose their jumps scares if you had a holographic representation of the entire scene and could see the monster hiding behind the bushes. So yeah, within our lifetimes, we probably are limited to only incremental improvements beyond our current technology. But our current technology is anything but a nightmare. It really is pretty amazing when you stop and think about it, and would have seemed like a technological marvel to people from just a century ago.

Could Kamala Harris beat Donald Trump? Yes. And Trump could beat Harris. Presidential elections in the past 30 years have all been relatively close. Roughly half the votes will go to either candidate, plus or minus a few percent that decides who will win (and a few more percent to third party candidates). And of course, that whole process gets filtered through the electoral college, so a candidate doesn't even need a majority of the popular vote to win the election. ABOVE SOURCE: United States presidential election - Wikipedia This year will be no different. Trump will get around half the vote. Harris will get around half the vote. Whoever performs best in the swing states will win the overall election. Sure, you've got plenty of people right now making 'guarantees' about who will win. And given that it's really a binary choice, a lot of those people will inevitably end up picking the eventual winner. But it doesn't mean they actually had any better insight than the rest of us. It means they just got lucky by calling the coin toss. I think we can safely predict, at least, that Robert Kennedy is not going to win. Side note: I don't mean to discount polling as worthless. I think it still is useful and valid as long as you understand it's limitations. It's just that polling can't tell you much when elections are decided by less than the polling margin of error. Another side note: This question is from 2016, but for obvious reasons, it's taken on a new found relevance.

What is the probability that a satellite the size of the moon, would orbit just the right distance from a planet the size of the earth, that from the planet, it appears the same size as a star the size of the sun, at its distance from that planet? The Milky Way contains somewhere between 100 billion and 400 billion stars, and probably at least that many planets. I’m sure there are interesting coincidences of some sort or another in practically all solar systems. On our planet, it happens to be a moon that appears to be roughly the same size in the sky as the Sun. On other planets, there are probably different coincidences that we don’t enjoy here. On the other hand, I’ve seen claims like this one from NASA, that “The Moon makes Earth a more livable planet by moderating our home planet's wobble on its axis, leading to a relatively stable climate. It also causes tides, creating a rhythm that has guided humans for thousands of years.” So if large moons like ours are necessary for the development of civilization, then that leads to a bit of survivorship bias. The only planets with intelligent life with the scientific knowledge to ponder such things would be planets with large moons. Other planets without large moons, even if they had life, wouldn’t have stable enough climates to make civilizations possible. In other words, our planet having a large moon isn’t so much a coincidence, as it was a pre-condition for us to develop in the first place.

If the weight of a body in water is 12N and weight of liquid displaced by the body is 8N, then what is the weights of that object in air? This is a bit of a trick question. To overcomplicate it a bit, here are free body diagrams comparing when the object is underwater vs. above water (with the force arrows obviously not drawn to scale): Weight is the same in each case. And of course that has to be the case, since weight is defined as W=mg. As long as the mass didn’t change, and you’re conducting these experiments from roughly the same location on Earth (so that g doesn’t change), the weight won’t change, either. Sure, if you wanted to be very precise about the net force, you could calculate the exact buoyancy force (hint: you should know or at least be able to look up the densities of water and air). But given that water is roughly 800 times denser than air, you know that the buoyancy force from air is going to be pretty negligible. Weight doesn’t change even when other forces are acting on an object. Buoyancy may change the net force, but not the weight.

Why are millenial and gen Z women so much likelier to wait until their 30s to settle down and are far more sleighted to want to sleep around with tens of people before earnestly looking for a partner? No shame, no blame. Just curious. While there may be less stigma towards sex outside marriage these days, the data doesn’t show that this has actually led to younger folks ‘sleeping around’ more. For example: ABOVE SOURCE: Millennials are cool with casual sex, have less of it And also: ABOVE SOURCE: A 'failure to launch': Why young people are having less sex And it intuitively makes sense. Baby boomers were the generation that went through the sexual revolution. So they were out there experimenting before the advent of comprehensive sex education in schools. They were the proverbial overprotected kids who went a bit wild with their first taste of freedom. Later generations have been a bit more reined in in their sex lives. Besides, I don't know if there is an ideal number of sexual partners for a person to have. I'm sure it varies by person. But 1 seems on the low side – no chance to get out there and gather different experiences. On the other hand, Wilt Chamberlain's claim of 20,000 seems on the high side – many of us still see sex as an intimate and emotionally significant act, and having thousands partners really diminishes that (not to mention the increased risk of spreading STDs). Anyway, returning to the question, Millennials and Gen Z don’t seem to be more likely to have more sexual partners than previous generations. In fact, it’s largely the opposite.

Scientists dabble and meddle in the genome with the intent to make life better, but are they really, intentionally or unintentionally, redefining or redesigning life? If so, how? People have been 'redesigning' life since the advent of domestication and selective breeding of crops and livestock. The big difference between that and intentional genetic engineering is that the old methods were haphazard, relying on willy nilly random mutations that nobody understood at all. It wasn't even until the last century or so that people even knew about genetics. So in the past, if somebody wanted to know if a new strain of crop that improved yield was also safe to eat, the only recourse was to eat enough of it to see what happened. Nowadays, we have enough of an understanding of the underlying genetics to already have an a priori idea of whether certain genetic changes will be safe or not. And we have more rigorous testing protocols for genetically engineered crops. Do I think such intentional genetic engineering can make life better? It certainly has the potential to do so. Take golden rice, for example. This is a new strain of rice engineering to have beta-carotene, a precursor to vitamin A, which can help drastically reduce Vitamin A deficiency in certain regions of the world where malnutrition is a problem. Or take Bt crops, so named for incorporating genes from the Bacillus thuringiensis bacteria, making proteins that are toxic to insects. This allows farmers to reduce the amount of insecticides they spray on their crops, with a secondary effect of reducing the greenhouse gas emissions from the equipment that does the spraying (FWIW, organic famers often spray a solution with the live bacteria onto their crops, since bacteria are 'organic'). ABOVE: A conventional rice variety on left compared to the more nutritious golden rice on right SOURCE: GM golden rice gets landmark safety approval in the Philippines So yes, genetic engineering is redesigning life, just like we’ve done for millennia, but in a much more controlled and less haphazard manner than traditional selective breeding. And yes, it certainly does have the potential to make life better. And if you were asking about the human genome, just ask anybody with a genetic disease if they'd like to be able to be cured. I lost a few childhood friends to cystic fibrosis. Genetic therapy would have been a literal life saver.

Have you ever met an intelligent creationist? I've met intelligent creationists, but never any creationists in person who actually understood evolution. Every time I talked to an intelligent creationist about how they thought evolution worked, I invariably found that they didn't actually understand. Their views tend to be a mish-mash of Lamarckism, teleological thinking, evolution being progression towards a goal, and human exceptionalism, along with a lack of knowledge of how evolution works, and even a lack of knowledge of modern day organisms. These types of misconceptions drive such questions as wondering why there are still monkeys if we evolved from monkeys (though it's never why there are still birds if penguins evolved from birds), or wondering whether the first fish to crawl onto land would have had either gills or lungs (totally ignoring all the existing fish that have both). You can browse through the Index to Creationist Claims to get an idea of the types of arguments creationists might use. I don't wholly blame these folks, either. They were raised in an environment where creationism was the default, from their parents to their preachers, to possibly even their school teachers (my daughter's high school biology teacher made an announcement at the start of the lesson on evolution that, as a Christian, she didn't believe in it, herself, but it was just part of the curriculum that they had to get through). They were taught all these misleading creationist arguments from people they trusted from a very young age. So the smartest kids were actually the best at absorbing those lessons. And since it takes a while for people to fully develop critical thinking skills, and a fair amount of discipline to go back and apply that to things you think you already know, it's hardly a surprise that those bright kids brought up within a creationist environment carried that belief into their adulthood. (And to be fair, ask yourself how you know that matter is composed of atoms and that atoms are composed of even smaller particles – do you really understand the evidence, or is it just common knowledge that you were taught back when you were younger?) I will say, though, that the number of intelligent, well-educated creationists I've met is rather small. You can definitely see a correlation vs. education level (note that graph is a bit old from 2005): SOURCE: Americans Weigh In on Evolution vs. Creationism in Schools So yes, I've met otherwise intelligent folks who were also creationists. But once you talk with them, it almost invariably turns out that, for whatever reason, they don't actually understand evolution. I have yet to meet a single person in real life who could accurately explain evolution yet still rejected it.

How many hours do you need to exercise to lose weight? Exercise is very important for overall fitness and health, but not so much for losing weight. And even the benefits it does have for weight loss are a case of diminishing returns. In other words, if you exercise an hour a week, that is better for weight loss than sitting around doing nothing. But exercising for two hours a week isn't going to double the weight loss benefit. Your body has a certain basal metabolic rate that it needs simply for surviving. Even if you do nothing but sit at a desk all day, you know you still need to eat. And this basal metabolic rate is actually the biggest energy expenditure for most of us, accounting for something like 60–80% of our calories. ABOVE: Components of total energy expenditure for an average young adult woman and man. SOURCE: Why you shouldn't exercise to lose weight, explained with 60+ studies But as we start doing more physical activity, our body compensates. In order to save energy to help keep our food requirements down (because historically, starving was a much bigger danger than obesity), our body reduces the energy put into the basal metabolic rate. ABOVE: The body adapts to increased physical activity by reducing energy spent on other physiological activities. SOURCE: Why you shouldn't exercise to lose weight, explained with 60+ studies As you can see in the figure above, going from a sedentary lifestyle to a moderate amount of exercise does substantially increase your total energy expenditure. But as you keep pushing the physical activity higher and higher, the compensation from our body causes the total energy expenditure to somewhat level off. Sure, if you're an elite athlete doing tons of training, you'll need more calories than most of us. But most of us aren't elite athletes. And the calorie counters on your Fitbit or treadmill aren't all that accurate to begin with, and don't take into account any drop off in your basal metabolic rate. So just because your Fitbit says you burned a certain amount of additional calories by tacking on another exercise, don't think that that justifies you consuming that many more calories. The Fitbit is likely wrong. So, exercise for your health and fitness. It really is the right thing to do. But when it comes to losing weight, pay attention to what you're eating, and eat less.

Are there any fossil remains of the fish that decided to walk onto land, thus becoming a man? Yes, but a couple clarifications, first. First, it's not like any fish personally decided to grow limbs that were closer to legs than fins. Mutation really is a random process beyond the conscious control of the organisms experiencing those mutations. Just think about yourself. Did you choose any of the genetic mutations that differentiate you from your parents? If you have any children, did you choose any of the genetic mutations that got passed on to them? No, of course not. Such mutations are things that happen on a chemical level that we're never aware of. Heck, us people are just about the only organisms with the smarts to even understand genetics in the first place, so our ancient fish ancestors certainly weren't thinking about genetic mutations. Second, evolution of such big transitions is a gradual process that takes many, many generations to happen. It's not like there was a fish species that instantly evolved into a land dwelling animal, let alone into us humans. There were many stages along the way, from 'walking' underwater (similar to frogfish or certain walking sharks in the modern day), to slightly amphibious lifestyles (like some catfish), to even more amphibious lifestyles (like mudskippers), to something that's finally fully specialized for a life totally on land. Here's a diagram showing some of the stages along the fish to tetrapod transition, with some extra detail on the limbs, and how these limbs gradually went through this transition from fully aquatic to amphibious to fully terrestrial: ABOVE SOURCE: The origin of tetrapods Here's another figure to give a sense of the transition from those first tetrapods to us people. One thing that can sometimes be a bit misleading about diagrams like this is showing just a single path, perhaps giving the impression that this path was inevitably leading towards us. But you could make diagrams like this for any living creature, e.g. the path to mosquitos, the path to dandelions, or the path to a mushroom. And even in this path, at any critter on there, if you weren't specifically interested in human evolution, you could go off in a different direction to look at other creatures. For example, from Orrorin around 6 million years ago, you could go down a different path that led to chimpanzees rather than us people. Or from that Repenomamus around 230 million years ago, you could pick paths to any mammal alive today. ABOVE SOURCE: Visualized: The 4 Billion Year Path of Human Evolution And just to be clear, all of the animals shown in both of those figures are known from fossil remains, sometimes more than one specimen for each species. Just going with the first figure, here are some of the available fossils: ABOVE: Eusthenopteron SOURCE: File:Eusthenopteron foordi 1.jpg - Simple English Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia ABOVE: Panderichthys SOURCE: Panderichthys | Fossiilid.info ABOVE: Tiktaalik SOURCE: Famous fish fossil takes final bow in Philadelphia ABOVE: Acanthostega SOURCE: File:Acanthostega Deep Time.jpg - Wikimedia Commons ABOVE: Ichthyostega SOURCE: Ichthyostega Fossil Skeleton, First Fish to grow legs & move onto land ABOVE: Tulerpeton (I couldn't find an actual photo in a quick Google search, but this at least shows which bones were actually found – in white, and which are only inferred – in grey) SOURCE: Tulerpeton curtum by Ivanbel on DeviantArt

Is Terrence Howard right that 1 + 0 = 1 and 1 x 1 = 2? I came across a recent video about this, posted just a week ago, and which has around 1.2 million views so far: What's a bit amazing is how many people in the comments seem to agree with him. I'm not sure how many are just trolling, but just in case there are folks who really are confused by this video and Howard's weird 'math', let's take a closer look. I'll start off this answer with super basic math, but then try to get into some discussion that's hopefully a bit more interesting. For those interested, Howard's book, which goes into even more detail, is available online for free: So let's start off with those basics, and why it really is true that 1×1=1, and not Howard's odd claim that 1×1=2. I apologize if all this seems rather basic, but one of the easiest ways to visualize multiplication is with grids of squares. Here are a few that I drew up in Excel. If you have a grid that's 3 squares by 2 squares, that can be written as 3×2, which is obviously 6 squares. If your grid is only 1×3, then you have 3 squares. And if your grid is 1×1, then it's just 1 square. This is all simple math and pretty obvious. Contrary to the way Howard seems to want math to work, a 1×1 grid does not produce 2 squares. Howard also seems to have a problem with multiplying by zero. He never actually proposes what he wants 1×0 to be, but this one's also pretty obvious from looking at grids. It doesn't matter how many hypothetical columns you have in your grid if it doesn't have any rows. 1×0=0 just like 10×0=0. Okay. Let's move on to something a bit more interesting – units. When you multiply real life things, you have to pay attention to the units. For example, even the video mentioned something about areas. Say you had a rectangle 1 ft × 1 ft. When you multiply those, you're not just multiplying the numbers 1 × 1. You're mutliplying (1 ft)×(1 ft). Or, to reorganize it just a bit, since you can multiply in any order, that's the same thing as (1×1)×(ft × ft), which gives an answer of 1 ft². And of course that makes sense. A 1 ft × 1 ft floor tile is one square foot, aka 1 ft². To get 2 ft², you would need two floor tiles, 1 ft × 2 ft. The video used an example of multiplying a penny by a penny. But this is something that doesn't make much intuitive or physical sense. What is it even supposed to represent? If you remember to pay attention to the units, it would be 1 ¢ × 1 ¢, or 1¢². But what is ¢² supposed to be? The value of money isn't measured in ¢², but just ¢, or more often $. (Or to use the video's exact nomenclature, 1 penny × 1 penny = 1 penny², but the unit of penny² doesn't correlate to counting pennies.) Let's look at an example of multiplying with money that makes more sense (lol). Say you had a bunch of boxes with 1 penny in each box. If you wanted to figure out how much money you had, you'd use a formula something like: (1 ¢/box)×(N box) Lets do a little bit of 'unit analysis' on that, going through a few steps of basic algebra: (1 × N)×((¢/box) × box) (1 × N)×(¢ × box / box) (1 × N)×(¢ × 1) N ¢ So the math works out to an answer that is just ¢, which is what we're interested in for the value of the money. If the units didn't work out that way, it would mean you had a formula that was calculating something else. So, to get back to Howard's claims, let's consider that we had one box: (1 ¢/box)×(1 box) = 1¢ So, the math works out to 1 ¢, which matches exactly what you'd already know without going through the math. One box with one penny inside is still just one penny, not two pennies. And just to be clear that this is multiplication, if you had a scenario with 2 pennies per box, and 3 boxes, you would have: (2 ¢/box)×(3 box) = 6¢ Or, looking at Howard's weird objections to multiplying by zero, if you had zero boxes, the math would be: (1 ¢/box)×(0 box) = 0 ¢ And of course, the math still works out. By not paying attention to units, Howard became even more confused when trying to multiply with pennies. A penny has a value of 1 ¢. But in different units, it has a value of $ 0.01. Those are the same value, because it takes 100 ¢ to equal $1. So even though it doesn’t make sense to multiply a penny times a penny, when you do legitimate math with money (like my box example above), pay attention to whether you're using $ or ¢ and don't get them mixed up. There's a tad bit more interesting discussion around his weird ideas around √2. First, he seemed a bit amazed that √2 + √2 = (√2)^3. But it's just a quirk of doing these calculations with 2, since adding a number to itself is the same thing as multiplying by 2. To do a tad more algebra, and understanding that √2 is simply another way to write 2^½: √2 + √2 2√2 2^(3/2) (√2)^3 Of course, that won't happen with any other number (besides zero), because when you add them together, you're not multiplying them by themselves. In other words, while √2 + √2 = 2√2, when looking at a different number √4 + √4 = 2√4, and not 4√4. However, if you add √4 together 4 times, √4 + √4 + √4 + √4 = 4√4 = 4^(3/2) = (√4)^3. So really, there’s a general pattern where you just have to add the numbers together the same number of times as the number itself. If you’ll indulge just a bit more algebra: x√x = x^(3/2) = (√x)^3 Going beyond just the video and looking at his book, Howard also lacked a full understanding of irrational numbers or how calculators work. He went off on one line of thought where he criticized the √2, because when you calculate it on a calculator, you get 1.414213562373095. If you multiply that number by itself on the calculator, the calculator will give an answer of 2. But when you multiply that number by itself by hand, you get 1.999999999999999861967979879025, which isn't actually 2 (I’m assuming his math is right – I didn’t double check him). This boils down to two things – first, irrational numbers can't be represented exactly by any type of fraction, including decimal notation. The string of digits after the decimal point is infinite (somebody calculated 10 trillion digits of √2 in 2022, which is still nothing compared to infinity). Second, calculators and computers don't have infinite memory, so they have to make do with approximating these numbers with a limited number of digits. But these approximations also apply to the answers of the math. So, when the calculator multiplies 1.414213562373095 by itself, the result of the algorithm is 2.000000000000000, because that's as accurate as the calculator can do it. So this is really just a limitation of calculators being tools to make pragmatic calculations that are accurate enough. There are very, very few cases where you would need a calculator to be accurate to more decimal places than that. For the types of scientists and engineers who do need that extra accuracy, they use special programs/computers to do so, but they still can’t calculate numbers to infinite decimal places. (FWIW, for my own day job designing airplanes, regular calculators and computer programs are more than accurate enough.) Most of the rest of the video (when it wasn't rambling about how profound all this was without actually explaining anything about it) was baseless nonsense, some of it from his failure to understand basic math, and some from wild conjecture without understanding anything about the fields he was talking about. If I wanted to respond to the rest of the video point by point, this answer would be huge (and it's already long enough), because just about every single claim is wrong. I mean, you can string words together into sentences that make grammatical sense, but that doesn't give them any credibility. I mean, he tried to say that sound will travel through space by 'inventing' something he called "the most wonderful vibrating preatomic geometry". But we've been to space, both actual astronauts and robotic satellite, probes, and rovers. We know for a fact that sound doesn't travel through space, despite Howard's fanciful imagination. Perhaps one of his points that might resonate with some people is that we humans can only see a small sliver of the electromagnetic spectrum with our own eyes, which is true. For what it's worth, that's also true of all other animals on Earth, because of the nature of how electromagnetic waves interact with matter based on the wavelength (see Bill Otto's answer to Is it possible for human eyes to work as an X-ray? for a more detailed explanation). But you know what we humans do have? Machines and instruments to detect things we can't see with our own eyes. That's how we know about the existence of the broader electromagnetic spectrum in the first place. I'm not saying humanity will ever know everything there is to know about the universe, but it's a bit ironic that Howard is using our ability to use science to detect things beyond our senses as a criticism of science. How would he have known how little of the electromagnetic spectrum we could see if it wasn't for science figuring that out? The video also closed with a bit of discussion of a fiat money system vs. the gold standard. Of course, the only reason the gold standard was valuable was because everybody agreed gold was valuable, not because of any intrinsic value of that particular metal. So a fiat money system is merely taking money one level of abstraction further, where everyone agrees to the value of the thing we call a dollar (or whatever currency another government uses). But there are plenty of other explanations of fiat money systems, so I'm not going to delve into that here. Anyway, that's as much as I'm going to write about Howard's ideas in this video and his book. I know that the basics of why his math is wrong are, well, basic. But hopefully the information I wrote about units and √2 was a bit more interesting.

Why do people seem to think gun control laws matter when in reality if I want to obtain a gun and the government thought it could stop me, I'd just obtain a gun through illegal means? This sounds like an argument against laws in general. If anything is illegal, I’ll just do it through illegal means. Of course, the whole point is that since it is illegal, law enforcement can catch you, and then you can be punished through the judicial system. That’s pretty much how all laws work. Do atheists actually believe they are monkeys? Do they have an urge to climb trees? Is it sad to only believe in one’s self? Let's take these one at a time: Do atheists actually believe they are monkeys? Meh. It's a semantics issue. I'm definitely an ape. And I'm definitely a primate, and definitely a mammal. And on and on for all the various larger taxonomic groups we're included in. But whether or not you think we're monkeys comes down to whether you think monkeys are a monophyletic, paraphyletic, or polyphyletic group. You can debate it, but it doesn't change the reality of the animals we evolved from. (FWIW, I have come around to thinking monkeys should be monophyletic, and that us apes are just a slightly specialized branch of monkeys.) ABOVE: Aegyptopithecus, which was a close cousin to our ancestors, and thus would have been very similar. SOURCE: Aegyptopithecus (note: the above image itself is valid, but Reptile Evolution is a bit of a dubious site - David Peters started off as a decent paleoartist, but kind of went off the deep end a couple decades back) Do they have an urge to climb trees? Yes. Don't you? I climbed trees all the time as a kid, and now that I'm an adult, it's only decorum (and aging joints) that keeps me from climbing them more often. But I still do climb trees from time to time. And when I got some scaffolding to do some work around the house, I told my wife it was like having a grown up jungle gym, and that it gave me an excuse to climb on it for 'work' instead of just playing around. Is it sad to only believe in one’s self? What does that have to do with atheism? I have eyes. I can see an entire world full of other people, animals, plants, etc. There's very much just here on Earth to believe in besides myself. And that's before you start looking at pictures of space, and the untold number of entire galaxies besides our own.

Who was the first ancestor of ours who walked on four legs? It depends on what you mean by 'walking'. It's also a bit cloudy because of the incompleteness of the fossil record. Let's address the definition of 'walking', first. Take a look at this video of a modern day creature (i.e. not our ancestor, and not even particularly closely related): I think it’s reasonable to say that it's walking along the coral reef, using its fins much like legs. And the truth is, walking underwater is a useful form of locomotion. Handfish and frogfish are also quite well known for walking underwater. And it seems that in our own ancestors, walking underwater came first, before any of them ever tried to crawl up onto a mud bank. I found an article that goes into great detail on the origin of tetrapods, The Fish–Tetrapod Transition: New Fossils and Interpretations. Here's a figure from that article, showing the relationships of species know from fossils, along with the general timeframe of when tetrapods evolved: ABOVE: Stratigraphic table of Late Devonian and Early Carboniferous with cladogram of tetrapodomorphs superimposed to show distribution in time. Broad bars show known range, narrow bars show possible range where exact dating is not available. Based on Ahlberg et al. (2008) SOURCE: The Fish–Tetrapod Transition: New Fossils and Interpretations Note that most of those are side branches, not our direct ancestors, so they're really only giving us a general idea of what our ancestors would have been like, not precise snapshots. Still, the first creatures to walk would have been along those lines. Here's another figure, with less animals, but with pictures of the ones that were included, including diagrams of their forelimbs: SOURCE: The origin of tetrapods - Understanding Evolution So, the first of our ancestors to walk underwater probably would have been something along the lines of Panderichthys. The first of our ancestors to spend an appreciable amount of time walking on land would have been something along the lines of Acanthostega. Though keep in mind the timeframes from the earlier figure, and that Acanthostega was living well after the actual first creatures to become so terrestrial. With recent finds over the past few decades, the current fossil record actually already is a lot more complete than when I was a kid. But there are still plenty of transitional species left to be found. I'm excited for scientists to find them so that I can learn about them.

Some worry that the United States is in an unusually anti-intellectual period right now. Is this really the case? Haven't societies always been composed mostly of people who are rather unthinking and just want "bread and circuses"? Like so many things in the modern day U.S., it's a partisan issue. Here's one graph with poll results going back to the mid '70s (note that the y-axis is compressed): SOURCE: Why Being Anti-Science Is Now Part Of Many Rural Americans’ Identity Historically, Democrats, Republicans, and Independents all hovered around close to the same trust in science at somewhere around 40%. In fact, for most of that period, Republicans had greater trust in science than Democrats, which is what you'd expect from the stereotypes of the parties when I was growing up (i.e. that the Republicans were the mature adults in the room, tempering the wide eyed enthusiasm of the idealistic but naive Democrats). But starting some time around the '90s, those historical positions began to reverse, with trust in science dropping among Republicans, while growing among Democrats. Today's Republicans have a historically low level of trust in science, while Democrats have an unprecedented level of support*. To those of us following the scientific side of the 'Culture Wars', the Republican collapse of trust in science isn't at all surprising. Folks were raising alarm bells around this issue back in the 2000s. Chris Mooney even wrote an entire book about the issue: ABOVE SOURCE: Amazon You saw it in global issues like climate change and local issues like evolution vs. creationism in the public schools. One very emblematic example came from our State Board of Education (SBOE) here in Texas, where the former chairman of the SBOE somewhat famously said, "Somebody's got to to stand up to the experts" (source: NCSE - McLeroy booted in Texas). Stop and let that sink in for a minute. The board of education thought it was their duty to go against the experts in the fields they wanted students to learn about. In more recent times, we saw the way this played out with the public response to COVID-19, in everything from how seriously people took the threat, to how willing they were to follow expert advice on mitigating the risks. And sadly, this had the follow on effect of a noticeable difference in death rates by party: SOURCE: Tomas Pueyo (@tomaspueyo) on X While there has always been a strain of anti-intellectualism within the U.S., the current trends are towards a sharper divide along political lines, with the Republican party becoming the anti-intellectual party. I wish this wasn’t a partisan issue. There's nothing inherent in conservative vs. liberal policies that makes this inevitable. It's just the unfortunate reality we live in right now. *I'm a bit cynical about the Democratic support of science. While I'd love for it to be authentic, I suspect it's mostly virtue signaling in opposition to the Republican distrust of science. But at least lip service in support of science is still better than organized opposition.

Question for atheists- how do you feel about Christians talking about their faith with you if they are nice about it (ie not screaming that you are going to Hell)? Do Christians in this manner bother you? I hope my question makes sense. I love it. I really, really like civil debates/arguments with friends. I mean, what's the fun in just agreeing about everything all the time? Especially when it comes to controversial subjects, these types of discussions are where we truly test our own positions. Do we really have a firm foundation for our beliefs? Have we really thought things through? I mean, it would be easy to only hang out in Internet echo chambers and just pat yourself on the back amongst folks who already agree with you, but that's where you run the risk of holding beliefs for superficial reasons. It's only when you test out your arguments among people who are going to challenge you that you can be sure that those beliefs are well founded. I also realize that atheists are still a fairly small minority in this country (USA), and that there's still a fair amount of stigma towards atheists. So by having these conversations, I can help to educate the person I'm talking to about atheism, and help de-stigmatize atheists. I can think of plenty of folks who were shocked to learn I was an atheist, because the stereotype of atheists in their mind was based on straw men and falsehoods. And just maybe, I'll plant some seeds of doubt about Christianity, helping them to see the light and embrace reality rather than ancient superstitions. I don't mean to imply that this is all one way street with me talking down to the Christians. It does me good to remind myself that not all Christians are like the con-men, hucksters, liars, and bigots that get so much publicity like Kent Hovind, Joel Osteen, Jimmy Swaggart, Benny Hinn, Ray Comfort, Fred Phelps, Robert Jeffress*, etc., etc. No, most Christians I meet in real life are just regular folks trying their best to live good lives, but it's hard to escape childhood indoctrination and cultural pressure. And I often learn things myself from these conversations. Perhaps not as much when it comes to religion (since I've studied it more than most of the religious folks I know), but certainly with many other controversial topics I'll argue with my friends about. And of course, everything in moderation. While religion is an occasional topic of conversation amongst me and my friends, it's not the only topic of conversation. There's a whole lot more to life that we spend more time on. As a real life example, just a few months ago, I had a couple Mormons show up in my driveway. They told me a little bit about their beliefs. I told them a little bit about the documentary hypothesis to explain the origins of parts of the Bible, and how Yahweh had developed from previous traditions within Canaanite polytheism. I'm not sure I convinced them of anything, but at least they knew I wasn't some stereotype who called myself an atheist merely because I was angry at God. It was all nice and friendly, and we were smiles and handshakes as they left. So yeah. I love conversations like these when they do happen. They're how we challenge ourselves and each other to be sure that our beliefs are well founded and robust, and they help to remind us that people who disagree with us on certain topics are still just regular folks. *I almost feel a bit guilty about Jeffress, since he used to head up a Baptist church here in Wichita Falls, where I live. Even though I never supported him while he was here, I still feel a tiny bit of guilt by association, that somehow we unleashed him on the rest of the world.

Is it better to fly two long haul flights (say 10 hours each) instead of one ultra-long haul flight (about 18-19 hours)? It depends a whole lot on your seats, which also depends on whether or not the flights are domestic or international (though I'm hard pressed to think of an 18 hour domestic flight*). I can think of three of my own experiences to help show the difference: I've never actually flown business class or first class on international flights, but I know people who have. If you can manage to get one of those seats, you'll definitely be fine. ABOVE: International business class seats often fold out into beds SOURCE: British Airways Business Class in Review: An Honest Report from A Seasoned Traveller In short, for domestic flights, if you're flying coach, try to break it up. As a native-English-language-speaker, is there ever situation in which you actually should not speak perfectly accurate English as defined by most academically approved English grammar and vocabulary books? I do it all the time, especially depending on how pedantic of a book you’re thinking of. In fact, I did it just there in that sentence, by ending it with a preposition. Sure, most modern style guides don’t include that rule, but it was something I was taught back in grade school. Ending sentences with prepositions often just flows better than other constructions. There’s also the old rule about not splitting infinitives. It’s another one that’s growing outdated, but you can still find style guides recommending against it, such as here: But again, sentences often flow better when you split the infinitive, so I’ve got no qualms with doing so. There are also times were ‘proper’ grammar sounds stilted or pompous. For example, I know when to use ‘whom’ vs. ‘who’*, but I usually go with ‘who’, anyway, to avoid the appearance of being pretentious. In other cases, there are words or phrases that I simply avoid, because the technically accurate meaning is not the same as the common usage. So if you use it the technically accurate way, a large part of your audience won’t understand you. And if you use it the common way, the pedants will jump on you. A good example of this is ”begs the question” – it doesn’t mean what most people think it means**. There are also cases where the incorrect grammar carries a certain connotation or emotional aspect that you wouldn’t get from proper grammar. “Say it isn’t so” just doesn’t sound as good as “Say it ain’t so.” Related to that last one are informal contractions, where there actually are slightly different shades of meaning. If I ask somebody, “What are you doing?”, it carries a connotation of the actual, specific actions they’re currently engaged in. If I ask, “Whatcha doin’?”, it’s more of a general inquiry. I could go on, but hopefully that’s enough examples to make the point. You definitely don’t want to overdo it, but there are still plenty of occasions to use informal grammar that wouldn’t necessarily be approved of by your English teacher. As a note of caution from someone who’s semi-fluent in a second language, myself, you have to really know a language well before you understand the rules well enough to know when it’s appropriate to break them. If you’re learning English as a second language, it’s best to just try your best to speak it as properly as you can, at least until you’re really, really comfortable with the language and slang. (BTW – did you notice that split infinitive, there?) *The Oatmeal has a useful comic on this: ** Okay, as more of a descriptivist than a prescriptivist, ‘what it means’ is what most people think it means. But you’ll still get complaints from the pedants.

Should creationism be taught in public schools as an alternative to evolution, given its religious roots, or does doing so infringe upon the separation of church and state? There are two aspects of this answer. First, of course teaching creationism in public schools violates the separation of church and state in the U.S. This has repeatedly been the interpretation of courts, from Epperson v. Arkansas back in 1968 to the more recent Kitzmiller v. Dover Area School District in 2005 (Ten Major Court Cases about Evolution and Creationism). But that's only a legal technicality. What if we didn't have the First Amendment, or lived in a different country that didn't enshrine the separation of church and state? Well, then we have the much more fundamental issue that creationism is wrong. I don't think many people realize that creationism was the dominant scientific paradigm prior to Darwin. Some naturalists may have toyed with ideas of 'transmutation', but they were largely seen as fringe eccentrics. At best, some naturalists were more in line with certain modern day creationists who concede evolution within 'kinds', but not universal common descent. It was the plausible theory and especially the evidence that Darwin presented in The Origin that basically convinced the scientific community practically overnight to accept evolution over creationism. In other words, those naturalists didn't reject creationism because they were a priori opposed to it, but because the evidence conclusively favored evolution over creationism. And in the 150+ years since then, the evidence for evolution has only grown even more overwhelming. So yes, teaching creationism in public schools in the U.S. would violate the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment. But even more importantly, creationism is factually incorrect and not good science, so why would you want to teach it to our children in the first place?
