What evidence supports the theory of natural selection and evolution as the origin of life on Earth, according to Charles Darwin? Well Quora Prompt Generator, this is actually a good question. While some of the strongest modern day evidence we have for evolution lies in DNA and the fossil record, DNA wasn't available at all to Darwin, and the fossil record wasn't anywhere near so well known, so Darwin had to rely on other forms of evidence to understand evolution and natural selection. You can get a quick overview just by looking at the titles of the chapters in his landmark book, On the Origin of Species: 1. VARIATION UNDER DOMESTICATION. 2. VARIATION UNDER NATURE. 3. STRUGGLE FOR EXISTENCE. 4. NATURAL SELECTION. 5. LAWS OF VARIATION. 6. DIFFICULTIES ON THEORY. 7. INSTINCT. 8. HYBRIDISM. 9. ON THE IMPERFECTION OF THE GEOLOGICAL RECORD. 10. ON THE GEOLOGICAL SUCCESSION OF ORGANIC BEINGS. 11. GEOGRAPHICAL DISTRIBUTION. 12. GEOGRAPHICAL DISTRIBUTION—continued. 13. MUTUAL AFFINITIES OF ORGANIC BEINGS: MORPHOLOGY: 14. RECAPITULATION AND CONCLUSION. In the first two chapters about variation, Darwin was looking at existing animals. One of his insights was the arbitrary distinction between 'varieties' and 'species', and that these distinctions weren't actually very clear cut. If species had been created separately and distinctly, you would expect identification to be straightforward. But if species were gradually morphing generation by generation, then you would run into these types of difficulties that Darwin identified. Rather than the differences in individual organisms being slight variations around a common archetype, there wasn't really any metaphysical archetype at all, nothing constraining what was 'normal' within a population or stopping the population from shifting over time. I'll also note that Darwin spent a lot of these chapters looking at pigeons, since those were a popular animal among breeders at the time, with lots of examples of different varieties and changes through breeding. The Struggle for Existence was more laying the groundwork to introduce natural selection. It seems rather obvious, now, but when you look at just how many offspring most organisms have, it's way, way more than what the environment can support (e.g. sea turtles lay hundreds of eggs each nesting season – if they all survived, the world would be quickly overrun by sea turtles). So, that necessarily means that the vast majority of organisms are killed without ever reproducing themselves, setting up an implicit competition. The fourth chapter is obviously where Darwin explicitly explained Natural Selection. Whether you want to count that as evidence or not, it was where he proposed a plausible framework for evolution. And the way science actually works in practice, you need that combination of evidence and explanatory framework to make a truly successful theory. The chapter on Laws of Variation looked once again to many types of living organisms, and the types of variation within populations – birds (and more pigeons, again), beetles, blind cave animals, various plants, etc., and especially the patterns of variation, and how those patterns were better explain by common descent than by special creation. Chapter 6 was about Difficulties on Theory. Darwin did highlight the lack of known transitional forms in the fossil record at the time. This is also the chapter that includes the statement loved by creationists, that the evolution of the eye "seems, I freely confess, absurd in the highest possible degree." However, for each of the potential difficulties he raised, he went on to offer responses and potential mitigating reasons, and still kept his conjecture based on evidence from living organisms (e.g. even though he got it a bit mixed up, highlighting the similarity of swim bladders to lungs as a potential evolutionary pathway; though in truth, lungs actually came first and evolved into swim bladders). And in the case of the fossil record, he's certainly been vindicated, as more extensive study in the century and a half since he published that book has found innumerable transitional fossils. In fact, one of the best examples, Archaeopteryx, was discovered in 1861, just 2 years after he published The Origin in 1859. Darwin himself noted that the chapter on Instinct could have been included in the previous chapter, but he decided to give it a fuller treatment. And again, his approach was to show plausible scenarios for adaptations that might at first blush seem too far fetched. He even introduced the idea of kin selection, "that selection may be applied to the family, as well as to the individual, and may thus gain the desired end." The next chapter was about Hybridism, and taking a close look at fertility and infertility when hybridizing organisms from different species and varieties. This was an in-depth analysis to support his previous point of the distinction between species and varieties not being clear cut, which is what you'd expect from common descent. The next two chapters dealt with the geological record. The first of these two was a more detailed treatment of the issues raised in Chapter 6 about the incompleteness of the geological record, while explaining what was known at the time. As far as evidence, this was obviously pretty heavy on geological strata and formations. The next chapter built on that, synthesizing the facts previously laid out and introducing a few more fossils to explain how the evidence that did exist was entirely consistent with and indicative of common descent. Moreover, and perhaps based on his time on the Beagle, he described how fossils in different regions were more consistent with each other and the still living life in those regions, rather than other regions. If creatures had all been created rather than evolved, why would you see this pattern of regional similarity? The next two chapters were some of the lines of evidence that impressed me the most – Geographical Distribution. This built upon the idea touched on in the last chapter, of the similarity of organisms in certain regions compared to different regions, even when two regions may have broadly similar habitats. To give one striking example of two similar habitats that were even extremely close to one another yet geographically isolated, "No two marine faunas are more distinct, with hardly a fish, shell, or crab in common, than those of the eastern and western shores of South and Central America; yet these great faunas are separated only by the narrow, but impassable, isthmus of Panama." Some of my favorite bits of evidence from this chapter come from experiments Darwin did himself to try to better understand the ways in which seeds could be dispersed to spread the range of particular species. In one experiment, he immersed several types of seeds in salt water, periodically pulling some out and planting them, to see how long the seeds could survive such conditions (up to months in a few cases). In another, and getting his hands a bit dirtier, "In the course of two months, I picked up in my garden 12 kinds of seeds, out of the excrement of small birds, and these seemed perfect, and some of them, which I tried, germinated." In those chapters on geographical distribution, I was especially struck by his observations and data of the life on oceanic islands. Islands (or at least some of them) are self-contained, isolated habitats. From the framework of special creation and the immutability of species, the types of life on them could be anything the creator desired, and you might suspect a sort of specialized island ecosystem that was the same from island to island no matter where on Earth. But the reality is that life on islands is most similar to life on the nearest mainland, without actually being the same species. Moreover, the kinds of life on islands isn't just a representative subset of mainland life, but is biased by certain other considerations. For example, Darwin specifically noted that no mammals were ever found to be indigenous to islands more than 300 miles away from a continent, while they were indigenous on islands closer to continents. Darwin's key insight in all this was that these patterns are explained by life arriving at islands from the mainland, and then evolving to adapt to their new island life once there. The bias is explained by the types of animals that can survive the journeys. That puts birds and flying insects as very likely island inhabitants (for example, getting caught by the winds of a storm), while cold blooded animals with low food needs could survive long 'rafting events' on vegetation mats or floating debris, while mammals with their high food needs could only survive short journeys. The chapter on Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings looked at the well known similarities in the anatomy of various organisms, and how those similarities naturally form into nested hierarchies. He went into details such as homologous organs, vestigial features, embryology, etc. I haven't quoted much from Darwin throughout this answer, so here's a bit of a longer excerpt where he gets a bit more excited than normal (he used an exclamation mark): How inexplicable are these facts on the ordinary view of creation! Why should the brain be enclosed in a box composed of such numerous and such extraordinarily shaped pieces of bone? As Owen has remarked, the benefit derived from the yielding of the separate pieces in the act of parturition of mammals, will by no means explain the same construction in the skulls of birds. Why should similar bones have been created in the formation of the wing and leg of a bat, used as they are for such totally different purposes? Why should one crustacean, which has an extremely complex mouth formed of many parts, consequently always have fewer legs; or conversely, those with many legs have simpler mouths? Why should the sepals, petals, stamens, and pistils in any individual flower, though fitted for such widely different purposes, be all constructed on the same pattern? Of course, the explanation as put forth by Darwin is common ancestry, and modifying the anatomy of ancestors, rather than a creator creating organisms from scratch without constraint. The last chapter was just a summary (recapitulation) of the book as a whole, so not much for me to add in this answer as it pertains to evidence. So, that's a summary of the evidence for evolution and natural selection as according to Charles Darwin. The way we so often think of evolution as a study of the past, when I first read On the Origin of Species, I really was struck by how much Darwin relied on evidence from the present day and living organisms, and how he was able to infer common descent from the patterns in existing life. And even that was enough to convince most naturalists of his day of the truth of evolution. I think Darwin himself would be amazed to see just how many fossils people have found since then, and how many details later scientists were able to fill in.

Is English considered a foreign language to the US? Why can't most Americans speak English fluently or even close? As someone who has been learning English for about 3 months, I probably speak much better English than most Americans. Why? I'm going to focus on this part of your question: As someone who has been learning English for about 3 months, I probably speak much better English than most Americans. No, you don't. I studied Spanish pretty extensively in high school and college, to the point of being only 2 classes away from a Spanish minor*. I could speak fairly fluently. Then, after I graduated, I met the woman who was to become my wife, who happens to be Mexican with a large Mexican family (all living in the U.S.). I could catch them making grammatical 'errors' that weren't 'proper' Spanish**, and I could definitely spell Spanish words better than them (they mostly grew up in the U.S., so didn't have much formal education in Spanish). But my way of speaking Spanish was much more academic and stuffy, and just didn't flow the same way. Nobody would have confused me as speaking better Spanish than native speakers who had been speaking it their entire lives. Going the other way, I once made a business trip to China, and during the one day we set aside for sight seeing, I was approached by an old Chinese guy who wanted to speak to me in English, who turned out to be a retired English teacher. In other words, he was such an expert in the English language among the Chinese that he was teaching others how to speak English. But his English wasn't exactly the best. Don't get me wrong, his English was far better than my non-existent skills in Chinese, but it seemed obvious that he'd probably never been outside China and gotten to practice with actual native speakers. Even a lifetime of academic study isn't enough to make someone speak as well as a native speaker. Now, I really suspect you're a troll and not somebody who just began studying English 3 months ago. But people who aren't native speakers have to study a long, long, long time to become as proficient at the language as native speakers. And it really requires immersion in the culture, hearing the language day in and day out to pick up all the nuances and informalities that you simply can't completely learn any other way. On the off chance that you really are new to studying English, learn a bit of humility like I did when I met my wife’s family. Academic English is not the way real people speak, and it’s going to take a lot more than three months of studying in a school environment before you sound natural. *The reason I didn't just tack on two more classes was because I was already taking one Spanish class my final semester, and another two would have given me a very full load. So, instead, I tacked on a semester of Italian to learn a bit more of a different language. I figured the actual skill would serve me better than an additional piece of paper. **I put grammatical 'errors' in scare quotes, because I've come around to the idea of grammar being descriptive, not prescriptive. Who gets to decide what's proper and what's not. Where do they get off thinking they have that authority? Language has been around for far longer than scholars to study it, and people did just fine.

What's your go-to healthy snack when cravings hit? Single serve bags of potato chips: Because let's be frank. When it's an honest to goodness craving, rabbit food just isn't going to cut it. I see a bunch of other answers here trying to promote 'healthy' snacks, and while all those would be fine under normal circumstances when you’re merely peckish, they're just not going to satisfy a craving the same way junk food will. And I've tried. You eat the healthy alternative, and you're not satiated. You just want more. And if you eat enough until you're full, you've just eaten more calories without actually satisfying the craving. But a single serve bag of potato chips is only 1 oz of food, and only 160 calories. Sure, it's not the best thing to eat all the time. But every once in a while? That's not going to kill you. And it will actually satisfy your craving with all that starchy, greasy, salty goodness. And the fact that it's in a single serving bag makes portion control that much easier. With a full size bag, it's easy to just keep going back for one more chip, one more chip, one more chip, until eventually you've eaten a lot more than you should have. But if you know the one small bag is all you get, you eat your one serving and stop. The whole point is that a healthy diet is all about balance and moderation. And abstinence will just lead to worse cravings, or even falling off the healthy diet altogether. No single food in moderation is going to be all that bad for you. Just make sure to balance it out with enough other types of food to have a healthy diet overall. On days when the cravings aren't quite so bad to give in to potato chips, my next go-tos are pickles and olives (or olive salad on crackers). You still get enough saltiness to help satisfy the craving (and the olive oil from the olives), but not too terrible on the calories. After that is probably pita chips. Still starchy and salty, but not quite as greasy as the chips.

Can airplanes sometimes not store fuel in their tanks due to weight limitations? If this is the case, what are the alternatives for storing fuel in an airplane or other vehicle? Airplanes are much more weight sensitive than the cars that most people are used to. Cars have fuel tanks that will typically let you drive somewhere around 5 hours before needing to refuel. And you don't need to worry all that much about how much you load up your car. It can be just you driving by yourself, or loading up the whole family with luggage. Your gas mileage might go down a bit, but unless you're looking at really heavy cargo, you don't have to worry about overloading the car. Planes, on the other, don't have that luxury. You get a combined 'useful load', which is how much you can load up an airplane before it becomes too heavy to fly. It's up to the operator to decide how much of that useful load to devote to passengers and other payload, and how much to devote to fuel. Take the Cessna 172 as an example, one of the most iconic general aviation airplanes. It has 4 seats, a useful load of 878 lbs, and gas tanks that can hold 318 lbs of fuel. If you're running the math in your head, you can see that if you filled up the tanks with fuel, you'd only have 560 lbs of payload left, which may be fine if you're flying by yourself, but doesn't leave a lot of weight for 4 passengers and luggage, especially if they're adults. ABOVE: A screenshot from Cessna’s website, with appropriate text for a discussion about fuel burn SOURCE: Cessna Skyhawk Piston | Textron Aviation But, that 318 lbs of fuel is enough to let you fly for over 5 hours. Do you really need to fly that long if you're just taking some friends up for a sight-seeing flight around town, or for the clichéd $100 hamburger at the next airport over? Probably not. So, you might only load up half the fuel, which still lets you fly over 2 ½ hours, but leaves you 719 lbs for passengers and other payload, which is getting much more reasonable for 4 people (not necessarily 4 large adults, but at least a mix of larger and more petit folks). It's all about giving the operator options. You could make the full fuel payload seem higher by giving them a smaller gas tank, but then they wouldn't have the freedom to fly longer flights. Or you could just give it two seats, but then they wouldn't have the freedom to carry more passengers. So, you give them the ability to decide how they want to use the plane. For the big boys in airliners, it's a lot of the same considerations. Is it a short haul flight between close cities? Only load as much fuel as you need and then cram it full of passengers. Is it a long range flight? Well, you might have to go lighter on the cargo. So to answer the question directly, yes, sometimes airplanes don't fill up the wing tanks in order to be able to carry more payload. But other times it's the opposite, filling up the tanks and carrying less payload. It's all up to the specific mission.

According to the Bible, the earth is only 6000 years old. How does it explain the 4.49-billion-year gap between that and the actual age of the earth? Whenever questions like this pop up, poor Archbishop James Ussher is sure to unfairly come under fire for supposedly inventing the roughly 6000 year old age of the Earth out of some misconceived eccentric interpretation of the Bible. But really, that was a fairly mainstream view of the Bible at the time. While no passage in the Bible gives an explicit date for creation, if you take certain passages at more or less face value, you can come up with a reasonable estimate. Plenty of other scholars besides Ussher came up with their own estimates, and they all clustered around the same ages – either around 5500 BC if using the Septuagint as your basis for scripture (i.e. the Greek Old Testament), or around 4000 BC if using the Masoretic Text (i.e. the authoritative Hebrew version). Wikipedia lists many of these other scholars in its article on Dating creation, and it includes such well known names as Clement of Alexandria, Eusebius of Caesarea, Hillel, Johannes Kepler (yes, that Kepler), and Martin Luther, among many more. You can get a good part of the estimate pretty easily yourself by looking at just a handful of passages: The first two list genealogies from Adam down to Abraham, including the ages of how old the men were when their sons were born. The third states that Abraham was 75 years old when he left Haran for Egypt. The four is an explicit statement of the time the Israelites spent in Egypt before the Exodus, and the fifth is an explicit statement of the time passed from the Exodus until Solomon’s Temple. And that right there is enough to get you from creation to the Bronze Age in roughly 3000 years. Sure, there are a couple ages in there that are slightly ambiguous (particularly Noah and Terah), and also a bit of ambiguity about how long it took Abraham to travel from Haran to Egypt, but you're only looking at a few years of ambiguity there, nothing major. After that is where things get more intricate. You have to scour through the reigns of a bunch of kings of Judah and piece together that history (particularly from Judges, Kings, and Chronicles). And of course, that's exactly what Ussher (and all those other scholars) did, totaling up to around 430 years. That gets you to the accession of the Babylonian king Amel-Marduk, which from other historical sources was known to have taken in place in 562 BC. So, take the 3000 years from Adam to Solomon's temple, the 424 years of kings reigning in Judah, and 562 BC as a reference point, and you end up with a date for creation right around 4000 BC (4004 BC per Ussher). Now, I'm not a believer in the Bible, myself, so I take all this with a grain of salt since I don't think the Bible is a reliable source of history (particularly the older books like Genesis). But for those folks who do take the Bible seriously, this all seems perfectly reasonable. If you want to argue that the Bible doesn't indicate that creation took place in roughly 4000 BC, which of those portions are you willing to say is wrong? The reigns of rulers in Judah? The Exodus story? The otherwise boring and tedious recitation of fathers begetting sons? Given the mainstream view in Ussher's time of trusting the Bible to be historically accurate, I think he made a pretty good go of it. He just made the mistake of using an unreliable reference. (In fact, it’s precisely because he was so diligent and meticulous in his efforts that his particular estimate became one of the most respected in his time, and why it’s still remembered today.) As far as the OP's question about reconciling this age with the more accurate 4.5 billion year age of the Earth, I think the simple answer is that the Bible was a compilation from a more primitive people who simply didn't yet know any better. They certainly weren't dumb. It just takes time for humanity as a whole to build up our knowledge, generation by generation. As the saying goes, we only know as much as we do today thanks to standing on the shoulders of giants. Related:

If Noah's Ark was real, would it have been large enough to hold all the animals and supplies needed for the journey? Well, the story obviously isn't real. We know it developed from earlier Sumerian versions of the myth, and that even the Bible version is a blending of the Yahwist and Priestly versions of the story, with conflicting details right within the Biblical narrative. There's no archaeological evidence of such an event. And so, so many details are so ridiculously implausible that there's no way it could have happened as told in the Bible. So, right off the bat, playing a hypothetical game of 'what if', you're already having to make plenty of concessions or adjustments to try to bring the story into the realm of reality. So the question is, how fast and loose do you play with the details of the story to pretend that it’s real. If you want to include all animal species that couldn't have survived a worldwide flood, then it's just flat out impossible. Just consider how many different species there are of beetles, nematodes, ants, etc. And keep in mind that even plenty of aquatic organisms require specific conditions that wouldn't have existed in the flood waters, and so the ark would have required aquariums for those animals, as well. There's a very good article written all the way back in 1983, The Impossible Voyage of Noah's Ark, where somebody did take the time to try to figure out the actual implications of carrying every animal species. They determined the ark would have needed to hold a grand total of 3,858,920 animals. They also determined that the ark would have had 1,063,125 cubic feet of usable internal space (after accounting for structure), which would have left just 0.275 cubic feet of space for each individual animal. Sure, plenty of those animals were small, but they still need room to move around. And you still need their food on top of that. And provisions to access their enclosures for waste removal. Etc. In other words, this scenario is just flat out impossible. But creationists have a trick they like to use, pointing out that the Bible didn't use the word 'species', but 'kind', which they like to define as roughly equivalent to the genus level. In this view, for example, Noah wouldn't have had to take wolves, dogs, foxes, coyotes, and all the other canids. He could have just taken a breeding pair of the canine kind. And then after the flood, their descendants would go on to 'adapt' (because they can't use the word 'evolve') into all the different canids alive today. Of course, that would require a form of hyper-evolution much faster than anything that ever happens in reality. But it lets them come up with a semi-plausible hand-wavy explanation to save a literal reading of the myth (semi-plausible in the same way that getting bitten by a radioactive spider gives you spider powers). A good review of such an explanation using 'kinds' can be found here, Noah's Ark: A Feasibility Study (written back in 1996 – we're not talking cutting edge science required to debunk creationist nonsense). This article addressed what was essentially a feasibility study by John Woodmorappe based on these creative assumptions. Woodmorappe's estimate brought the number of animals down to a somewhat more manageable total of 'just' 15,754. This wouldn't actually be enough animals even to save every kind, but I already said we'd have to bend reality in some places to answer this hypothetical, so we'll just roll with it. So this scenario provides 67.5 cubic feet per animal. Consider that a small elephant requires 214 cubic feet of space for transport (not long term living), and that most animals will be much, much smaller, so this scenario does look like it's plausible to at least cram all the animals aboard. But even then, if you look to modern zoos, and the various requirements for actual long term living space, food storage, food preparation, waste removal, etc., there's still no way that you could keep that many animals alive in that type of space for that length of time (40 days per the Yahwist source, 150 days per the Priestly source). So to sum it all up, the answer is no. It's just flat out impossible if you're considering every single species of animal. And even if you play word games with 'kinds', while it might be physically possible to cram that many bodies aboard the ark, it wouldn't be under survivable conditions, or with anywhere near enough supplies to support the animals until the flood waters subsided. Hypothetically, let's say there is a world where Christianity is backed by mountains of evidence and all the stories of the Bible are verifiable and proven, would you still follow the teachings of Christianity or choose to live your own life? The problem is that this literally isn't possible. The Bible contains many, many contradictions, so you simply can't verify and prove all of the stories. The best you can do is verify some of the stories. And at that point, we're left to cherry pick which stories and lessons we want to say are proven in this hypothetical scenario. Just to go with one example, are we going with the God of Exodus 20:5-6, who threatens "punishing children for the iniquity of parents to the third and the fourth generation," or the God of Ezekiel 18:19-20, who says that "A child shall not suffer for the iniquity of a parent nor a parent suffer for the iniquity of a child; the righteousness of the righteous shall be their own, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be their own"? Because the former seems quite barbaric and not at all worthy of worship. The latter at least seems fair. Still, though, the overall portrayal of God in the Bible is not particularly flattering. You've got the massacre of Noah's Flood with its drowning of infants and children, the horrific treatment of Egyptian commoners and their slaves in the Exodus story (Jeff Lewis's answer to Can you cite the verses of some morality flaws in the Bible?), and then the whole fiery furnace of Hell for the grave sin of doubt. And that's just scratching the surface. So, given all the contradictions within the Bible, even as a hypothetical, you can't imagine a scenario where all of it was proven true. But even going with the overall general portrayal of God in the Bible, he's not a being deserving of worship.

If everyone around the world rides bicycles that generate electricity and store electricity, how much of humanity's electricity consumption can be offset? The short answer is not much. The long answer is complicated, depending on exactly what you mean by bicycles and how much freedom you'll allow in interpreting the question. The first thing to note, that many people don't seem to realize, is that pedaling to power a generator gets harder and harder the more electrical power you have to provide. They just see the wires, and seem to think that it's no harder than pedaling a free-wheeling bike. But once you try to actually create current with those wires, they create magnetic fields. And those magnetic fields make it more difficult to turn the generator. The more power, the stronger the magnetic field, and the harder it is to pedal. It all goes back to the conservation of energy, and the fact that you can't get something for nothing. Moving on, if you mean stationary cycles, where instead of moving, you're just driving a generator, then you're not going to get much energy at all. Loring Chien already went through the math in his answer. Even taking it to the extreme of people riding such machines for 12 hours a day every day, you only get 10% of the world's electric consumption (the average person can only maintain around 50 - 100 W continuously). And of course, that extreme scenario is not at all practical. You can't do your real job when riding a stationary bike. So if you cut people’s time down to a somewhat more realistic 1 hr per day to leave them time to do other things, then you’re looking at less than 1% of the world’s electric consumption. But even that’s over-estimating the net results. If people are going to perform that much physical exercise daily, their calorie requirements are going to go up. That means more food needs to be grown, stored, and transported, and all of that takes energy. How much of that energy comes from electricity vs. petroleum based fuel is dependent on how quickly EVs displace IC engines, but it’s certainly going to be something (and non-negligible when you’re talking about changes to diet on the scale of the entire world’s population). If you meant adding a generator to regular bikes that generated electricity during the course of normal riding, the numbers come out even lower. Recalling that you can’t get something for nothing, a generator that’s driven through a direct mechanical connection is going to feel like riding the brakes, with the braking force being higher the more power you try to generate. Alternatively, a wind powered generator is going to increase your drag, again forcing you to have to pedal harder. Basically, since you need power to propel the bike, you have to settle for only a fraction of the power that the person can generate going to the generator. That’s why existing generators on bikes are only used for very lower power applications like lights. In short, you’ll generate well, well short of even the 1% from the previous scenario. What about the power savings if everybody rode bikes instead of driving in cars? Now, you’re looking at a double impact, because bikes are much smaller than cars and so don’t require as much power. i.e. The benefit is not just in using human power, but in not needing as much power to begin with. Of course, if you’re just looking at electricity, this is going to be a bigger effect as EVs become more common. What makes this complicated to analyze is that cycling can only replace some uses of automobiles, not all of them, so you have to take that into account. Here’s one study, Ditching the car for walking or biking just one day a week cuts carbon footprint,. If we take CO2 as a proxy for energy consumption, that study found “If just 10% of the population were to change travel behaviour, the emissions savings would be around 4% of lifecycle CO2 emissions from all car travel.” Based on a couple other sources (the Energy Information Administration and the Bureau of Tranpsportation Statistics), transportation in total makes up 37% of U.S. energy consumption, while light-duty short wheelbase vehicles (i.e. cars) makes up 40.3% of that, or around 15% of the total energy consumption. So a 4% savings on automobiles is around a half percent total energy savings. But if you upped that “10% of the population” to “100% of the population”, and it scaled linearly to a 40% savings on car travel, you’d end up with a 6% savings in total energy consumption. That’s not exactly huge, but it’s not negligible, either. To sum up, none of the scenarios result in huge energy savings. Loring Chien’s calculation of people riding all day, every day, still only results in 10% of the world’s electricity requirements. Reducing people’s time on the bikes to 1 hr a day drops that to less than 1%. Putting generators on existing bikes for transportation generates an even smaller percentage than that. The most realistic and achievable scenario is to get people to ride their bikes instead of driving their cars for trips where it’s feasible. Depending on how many people you can get to do this, you’re looking at around 0.5% total energy savings in a more feasible scenario, or 6% in an overly optimistic scenario. But a few percent here and a few percent there can eventually add up to significant savings.

If “burger” now includes fish and chicken sandwiches instead of only ground meat patties, what is the boundary between burgers and other sandwiches? In American English, 'burger' on its own most certainly refers to a ground beef patty on a bun. You can stretch the definition a bit by adding a description of some other ingredient besides beef, such as a chicken burger or a veggie burger, but the implication is that it's still a ground food of some sort formed into a patty. For example, this is a chicken burger. Note the ground chicken formed into a patty: ABOVE SOURCE: Natasha's Chicken Burgers While this, since it contains a whole piece of chicken that's been breaded and fried, is a chicken sandwich: ABOVE SOURCE: The OG Chick-Fil-A Sandwich Where you can run into a bit of a gray area is a ground beef patty that's not on a bun. If you put the patty in between two slices of grilled bread with cheese, then it's a patty melt. And then it's just a question of semantics as to whether or not you think a patty melt is a type of burger or something separate. The article I copied that image from does refer to it as a specific type of burger, and I tend to agree since the defining feature of a hamburger (with it’s origins from a Hamburg steak) is the ground beef patty. ABOVE SOURCE: This Is Why Whataburger Patty Melts Are So Delicious - Mashed Yes, I know that in some other countries, practically anything on a bun is referred to as a burger. I was a bit surprised (and relieved) one time going to a get together with my German friends, when they said they were going to make chicken burgers, but they were actually making what I would call chicken sandwiches. So to answer your question, in American English, the boundary between a burger and other sandwiches is using a ground meat (or veggie) patty. No patty – no burger.

If you believe the Bible is fiction, then why would anyone want to write such a work? It's not fiction in the same sense as a novel, where one person sat down to write a story. Much of what ended up in the Bible were legends and stories that had been floating around in that culture for generations, spread largely by word of mouth and oral history. Sure, every once in a while some scribe might have written down a particular version of one of the legends, but these wouldn't have initially taken on the authority of 'scripture', and the legends would continue to develop within the larger society. As a more modern day example, consider Grimm's Fairy Tales. The Brothers Grimm didn't invent these stories themselves. They went around collecting stories from German folklore. You can see this in the books now referred to as the Pentateuch (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy). By using critical analysis to study these books, it's clear that they were the result of combining four prior traditions, now known as the Yahwist, Elohist, Priestly, and Deuteronomist sources, with a round of editing by a person or group known as the Redactor. As just one example from the Old Testament, the Noah's Ark story can trace its origins back to older Sumerian flood myths such as Gilgamesh and Atrahasis. And even the story within Genesis is an intertwining of the Priestly and Yahwist traditions, with conflicting details throughout the story, such as the number of animals to take aboard (one pair of each kind vs. seven pairs of the clean kinds), how long the flood lasted (40 days in the Yahwist source per Genesis 7:17 vs. 150 days in the Priestly source per Genesis 7:24), and twice repeating that Noah went into the ark (7:7-9 and again at 7:13-16). The New Testament development was a bit more rapid, but it was still the result of stories being passed along by word of mouth for decades before a few educated converts to Christianity decided to write them down. Some of those accounts eventually acquired enough of a reputation to be included in the official canon, but many more never acquired the status of 'scriptures', and are regarded as merely early Christian writing. Basically, it's the same as many other mythologies. Nobody necessarily sits down with the intent to create a story from scratch. It's stories that get passed on orally from generation to generation, that develop and morph over the years. Some scribes write down the stories from time to time, and the written versions that strike a chord become canonical.

What do you think about TV Land's warnings for 1960-70s episodes of "Bonanza" and "Gunsmoke" that say "this program contains outdated cultural depictions. Viewer discretion is advised." Do you think this is necessary? First off, this question hits one of my pet peeves – using the word 'necessary' without any context, implying that 'necessary' is some intrinsic property all on its own. It isn't. Just about every time this word is used, it's in relation to a specific outcome. For example, are fermentable sugar and yeast necessary ingredients? Yes if you're making beer or bread. Not so much if you're grilling a steak. Considering that TV itself isn't a necessity, hardly anything around the medium is necessary in any universal sense. It all depends on what outcomes you want. So, if you're asking if these disclaimers are necessary – necessary for what? If you wanted to be cynical, you could say that the purpose of these disclaimers is merely a way to silence the busybodies with a token message that only lasts a few seconds, that most viewers will forget about almost as soon as the action starts. The network can still show controversial or 'problematic' content essentially unaltered, retaining most of the audience that enjoys those shows (and their associated advertising dollars). The networks have balanced the conflicting influences of alienating more politically correct viewers to losing more old fashioned viewers, and figured these disclaimers were the best compromise. It's the free market at work. If you want to be more charitable about their motivations, such disclaimers do play at least a small part in consciousness raising. It may only be a short message, but at least it's putting it in people's heads that these depictions may not be so benign. And so when they do watch these shows, they're not just uncritically accepting such depictions as right or normal. I think this is especially true when it comes to kids watching TV. I know, some folks like to say that parents should be aware of all the media their children are consuming. That's a bit unrealistic, not to mention a bit questionable advice in its own right. Such constant supervision has taken on its own derogatory term these days – helicopter parenting. On the other extreme, you have folks fondly remembering the 'good old days', when kids roamed their neighborhoods unsupervised for hours on end (and believe me, even back then, we found parents' stashes of 'questionable' media hidden in boxes in the attic). Ideal parenting is somewhere in between – a balance of oversight and child independence, where parents have a general idea of what their kids are up to, but not necessarily screening each and every TV show their kids are going to watch. And in this context, such disclaimers are important in the consciousness raising of children, who don't have the background and experience to fully understand such shows like adults. So yes. I think these disclaimers serve a purpose. They help in the consciousness raising of both nostalgic older viewers and younger first time viewers. And considering that it's such a short message and that the shows themselves are unaltered, it seems that it's only the most easily offended who get worked up about these disclaimers, anyway.

Think of a small submarine 10 miles deep in the ocean, 1 gallon of water now drives a generator at 80k PSI, then energy is used to separate hydrogen from water and moved to the surface for use. Any holes in this thought experiment? I don't see any 'holes', per se. It just doesn't seem practical for any real world purposes. If I understand the description in the question, you'll end up with something like this on your sub: You've got a tank big enough to allow 1 gallon of sea water to drive a turbine to generate power, and that power will be used for electrolysis to create hydrogen and oxygen. Pressure can be thought of as energy per volume: So, just rearranging a bit, energy is pressure times volume. You need some type of pressure differential to get any work out of that, which is why the contraption has that tank at atmospheric pressure in the diagram above. But since atmosphere pressure is so much lower than the water pressure that deep, we can just assume it's negligible. Anyway, assuming everything was 100% efficient (which it won't be), using the correct value of 16k psi for the pressure in the deepest part of the ocean, and that I’ve done all my math properly, that 1 gallon of water has a potential energy of 308k ft-lb or 0.156 hp-hr, or in terms more familiar to folks who aren't U.S. based engineers, 418 kJ or 116 Wh. In contrast, a AA battery has roughly 3.9 Wh. So your device, at most, has the potential to generate as much energy as 30 AA batteries. In actuality, after all of the efficiencies are accounted for, it will be even less than that. I think your sub is going to need more than 30 AA batteries worth of energy to complete its mission, so you're spending more energy to perform this mission than what you get out of it. So, while this device could theoretically generate hydrogen in principle, there are far more practical ways of generating power.

If you are an atheist, how do you explain conscience to yourself? As for YOU, where does it come from? Our innate morality is an evolved instinct as a social animal. Depending on the conditions and the niche, social groups can offer animals synergistic benefits greater than the sum of the individuals. So, you see various levels of social cooperation in all types of packs, herds, tribes, troops, pods, etc., with ants and bees being some of the most extreme examples. Individuals living in such social environments need social instincts, not just to make the group successful, but, and this is the really important part in regards to evolution, so that they're accepted into the group so that they can take advantage of the group benefits for themselves. If you ever watched the show Meerkat Manor, you may recall that meerkats kicked out of the group had much, much worse chances of survival than meerkats living in the group, so there's a very strong selection pressure for meerkats to have instincts that keep them in the group with all the benefits that provides. But it’s not a hippie dippie love fest. There are also conflicting instincts to not be too selfless to the group, lest an individual sacrifice their own reproductive success. Conversely, all members of the group have an interest in identifying and punishing freeloaders and cheats, since they would drag down the success of the group as a whole. Along those same lines, individuals will have an interest in not doing things that would mark themselves as cheats, themselves, to avoid punishment. So, social animals evolve a whole range of complex and sometimes conflicting impulses to maximize their success in such settings. Even actions that go against their own short term self interest may be important in maintaining their long term acceptance within the group. Of course, most of us aren't so Machiavellian and calculating in our own behavior and internal thought processes, but, anthropomorphizing what is in fact a mindless process, natural selection was when it instilled those instincts in us. And so that brings us to where we are today. Perhaps it's easiest to understand the impulses towards selfishness and nepotism for the more direct benefits they would seem to bring us and our offspring. But empathy and conscience are just as important for social animals, since they're critical to our acceptance into social groups and the benefits we get from living in those groups. Note: This answer was adapted from a previous answer: I'll also note, that in the interests of brevity, I didn't even get into topics like kin selection, which add another layer of reasons to cooperate and have feelings of empathy.

Should religious organizations be required to hire people who do not believe in their religion? It depends on the circumstances. In general, no. If it's a purely religious organization focused on purely religious pursuits, then the First Amendment is clear, and if they want to hire only religious folks, they're free to do so. If, however, it's an organization that drifts into more secular pursuits, things can get trickier. The issue is that bigoted folks can try to use religion as an excuse to avoid the same laws that apply to everyone else. Are they sincerely religious, or are they just using religion as a cover? Does it matter? I know that things have changed in the largest Mormon denomination, but up until the 1970s, racism and segregation were baked right into official church doctrine. Would it really be fair to let, say, a homeless shelter or a food bank discriminate against black people because the people running it didn't want needy black folks mingling with needy white folks? Personally, I don't think so. I think that a homeless shelter or food bank are moving enough away from religion and into secular pursuits that they should have to follow the same laws as everybody else. I know. The above isn't a perfect example for this question since it addressed who the organization served, not who the organization hired, but I think it's still helpful. Basically, if the scope of your organization is purely religious, then you can discriminate against people outside your religion as much as you want. But if your organization starts moving beyond religious pursuits into the broader world, at some point you'll be expected to follow the same rules as everybody else, and not fall back on your religion as an excuse for bigotry.

Why has Quora devolved into a toxic cesspool? For just about any question that starts with, "Why has Quora...", the answer is almost always money. I didn't get started on Quora back at the very beginning, but I still got on early enough to get a taste of what it was at its best. I mean, you still got people like Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton contributing answers when I first started using the site. But as great as Quora was back then, it was operating at a loss. It was living off of the cash from investors, trying to build up its userbase and reputation so that it would eventually become profitable. Those investors weren't putting their money into Quora just for fun. They want to see a return on their investment. And operating a social media site is expensive. Googling it just now, it has something like 400 million active monthly users. That takes tons of hardware and bandwidth, which costs tons of money. So, if Quora wants to start turning a profit, they have to find ways to reduce costs and increase the things that bring in money. And bringing in money mostly boils down to advertising, which means getting people to 'engage' with the platform. So, the questions Quora's management asks aren't how changes will affect the user experience, but how they'll affect the bottom line. And cutting down on moderation is an easy way to cut costs. Can a negative user experience drive some people away from the site? Sure. But you're still here asking questions, and I'm still here answering them. And according to Semrush.com, it looks like Quora's traffic has just continued growing over the past 6 months, despite all of us users complaining about the decline in the user experience (accessing stats going beyond 6 months cost money that I'm not going to spend just to answer this question): In short, the user experience on Quora has declined because it saves Quora money by not having to pay as much for moderation, while it doesn’t seem to have had a big impact on the engagement which brings in the ad revenue.

I'm not convinced any non-theistic worldview is true because non-theists haven't provided any evidence. I can't make myself believe something without evidence, so can any non-theist please provide evidence that any non-theistic worldview is true? You've got a weird way of approaching this question. Take fairies, for example. As you said, if you "can't make [your]self believe something without evidence", and there's no compelling evidence for the existence of fairies, the default position is to lack belief in fairies, or to take a non-fairiest worldview. If you needed some type of positive evidence for the non-existence of fairies, you'd be stuck in some weird ontological limbo. With no evidence for the existence of fairies, you couldn't believe in fairies, but with no evidence against the existence of fairies, you couldn't believe in their non-existence. But it's not just fairies. This goes for anything. You can build up positive evidence for the existence of something. It's much, much harder to build up evidence for the non-existence of something. That's why the burden of proof has developed the way it has. In general, it's up to the person claiming that something exists to prove their case. The rest of us have no need to take their claims seriously until they have such evidence. To borrow a somewhat silly example from the Internet, do you have any evidence against the existence of Eric The God-Eating Magic Penguin? Wouldn't it seem a bit ridiculous to say that just because you can't find any evidence against Eric, that you're not going to take the non-Ericist position? I hope you see where this is going. If gods exist, the burden of proof is on the people claiming that they exist. Until they can provide compelling evidence, the rest of us are under no obligation to take their claims seriously. Just like with fairies, the lack of evidence makes the default position a non-theistic worldview.

What is the main ingredient in a sandwich? In many cases, there isn't a single main ingredient. All of the ingredients are important and work together in harmony. Take perhaps my favorite sandwich (and it's a fierce competition, since so many sandwiches are so damn good), the BLT. IMAGE SOURCE: BLT (Bacon, Lettuce and Tomato Sandwich) It's only five ingredients – the bacon, lettuce, and tomato that the name implies, plus toast and mayo. Screw up any single one of those ingredients, and your sandwich is hosed. And believe me, I've had hosed BLTs where restaurants tried to 'dress it up', only to ruin the balance. Things like using ciabatta instead of sliced bread, piling what seems like an entire pound of bacon onto a single sandwich, or using some trendy lettuce instead of a nice, crispy iceberg lettuce. You've got to get all of the ingredients right, and in the right balance, or the sandwich just isn't the same. Even something like a hoagie, which may seem like just piling ingredient on top of ingredient, still relies on getting all of the individual ingredients right. I once wrote an answer explaining how Subway sandwiches are only mediocre in comparison to real hoagies (Jeff Lewis's answer to Why don't people like Subway subs?), and posted this image for the comparison: Just at a glance, you can see the difference between the sterile excuse for a sandwich in the top left compared to the other three proper hoagies. And it’s not just one thing that makes the difference. Good hoagies need to get every single ingredient right, from the bread to the meats to the cheese to properly shaved onions. All of the ingredients are important. Good sandwiches don't have a single main ingredient. Every ingredient works together to make a sandwich what it is.

When a particle collides with an antiparticle, they are transformed into energy, Is it true that matter is annihilated and destroyed? Is this literally true? Matter is destroyed? Doesn't this completely contradict the law of conservation of matter? Scientific laws aren't exactly ironclad dictates that apply across all conditions throughout the entire universe. They're short expressions or formulas that are useful as long as you understand their limitations. Take Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation, for example. It's extremely accurate at the scale of everyday interactions in our lives. It's still accurate enough to predict the orbits of most of the planets to within the precision of our ability to measure them. But it's not quite accurate enough to predict the orbit of Mercury, given Mercury's close position to the Sun. For that, you need Einstein's updated theory of gravity, General Relativity. But even though we know Newton's law of gravity isn't perfect, we continue to use it since it's still plenty useful and accurate for many applications. Another law that I used quite regularly in my own field of aeronautical engineering is the Ideal Gas Law. We know for an absolute fact that real gases don't behave exactly the same way as this law. But for the pressures I normally deal with for aeronautic applications, it's good enough: It's the same thing with the Law of Conservation of Mass. It also is extremely accurate at the scale of everyday interactions in our lives, enough that many of us engineers use it for things like designing airplanes or balancing equations for chemical reactions. But we also know that it's not accurate over all conditions. As Einstein famously pointed out, E=mC², based on the fact that mass and energy are fundamentally the same thing, and can be converted from one to the other. And while this applies to everything, the difference in most everyday situations is negligible (a warm can of soda will be ever so slightly more massive than when it was cold, but your kitchen scale isn't anywhere near sensitive enough to measure the difference). So, the issue is that you're trying to apply the Law of Conservation of Mass to a condition outside where it would be valid. Instead, you need to look at the broader law, Conservation of Mass-Energy. Keeping it to still simple terms, this basically boils down to: E 1 + m 1 C 2 = E 2 + m 2 C 2 If m2 < m1, it just means that E2 has to be increased to compensate. But the total value on each side of the equation has to be the same. Nothing is being lost or destroyed, just converted.

How can I share the life eternal with those that refuse to view it today? It is like giving someone a check for a billion dollars and they refuse to cash it. You’re right. It’s almost exactly like that. Anybody can write out a check purported to be worth $1 billion. But as soon as you try to cash the check, it will bounce, and you’ll realize it was just an empty promise or even an intentional lie or scam. And your bank might even charge you a fee for their inconvenience. You’ll have gotten your hopes up, only to be in the same financial situation or maybe even a little bit worse than before you received this check. If a random person offers you a $1 billion check, my advice is that you refuse to cash it. Of course, in the case of an afterlife, once you die and cease to exist, you won’t realize that it was an empty promise or a scam. But if there are strings attached (and with religions, there usually are), you’ll still have wasted at least some opportunities in the one life we actually do get.

Where does the concept of the Earth being six thousand years old come from? Is it from the Bible? It really does come from the Bible, if a bit indirectly. There are several passages in the Bible that give information on such things as how old people were when they had children or how long certain periods lasted, that if accepted at face value, can give a very close approximation of when Adam and Eve were created (according to the stories, at least). There are a few places where things get somewhat murky, but not enough to change things by more than a few decades* – nothing on the order of millions or billions of years. This was a fairly well accepted interpretation for generations, and many scholars made their own estimates of when creation would have taken place, including Johannes Kepler. Arguably the most respected of these was the estimate done by James Ussher, who put much effort into sorting out the murky periods. It's because Ussher's chronology was so well respected that it was included in the introductory material to several printed Bibles, including the famed Scofield Bible. Wikipedia gives a good summary of how Ussher made his estimate (Ussher chronology - Wikipedia). He broke it down into three periods: Using other sources outside the Bible, Ussher determined the enthronement of the Babylonian king Amel-Marduk to have occurred in 562 BC, which was tied in to the end of the Babylonian Captivity through 2 Kings 25:27. From there, it was just a matter of going backwards by all the years previously calculated, putting creation at 4004 BC. Creation to Exodus You can easily look up Genesis 5 and Genesis 11 for yourself, but to give an idea, here's the start of Genesis 5: This is the list of the descendants of Adam. When God created humans,[a] he made them[b] in the likeness of God. 2 Male and female he created them, and he blessed them and called them humans[c] when they were created. 3 When Adam had lived one hundred thirty years, he became the father of a son in his likeness, according to his image, and named him Seth. 4 The days of Adam after he became the father of Seth were eight hundred years, and he had other sons and daughters. 5 Thus all the days that Adam lived were nine hundred thirty years, and he died. 6 When Seth had lived one hundred five years, he became the father of Enosh. 7 Seth lived after the birth of Enosh eight hundred seven years and had other sons and daughters. 8 Thus all the days of Seth were nine hundred twelve years, and he died. It goes on and on like that. So, as long as you accept these statements as true, it's mostly a simple matter of adding up how old each man was when he begat his heir. The only real hiccups are between Noah and Shem, and between Nahor and Terah. Both of these are somewhat ambiguous. In the former, the passage states, "After Noah was five hundred years old, Noah became the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth." In the latter, the passage is, "When Terah had lived seventy years, he became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran." People who care about this issue more than I do have gone into detail to try to pinpoint those ages (e.g. Contradictions: Noah’s Three Sons). You also need to know how old Abraham was when the Exodus occurred. His age at the start of all those events comes from Genesis 12:4, "So Abram went, as the Lord had told him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran." I ran the math myself with a spreadsheet, and came up with 2049 years from the creation of Adam to the birth of Abraham, plus another 75 years until the Exodus, for 2124 years total (a bit different from Ussher because I didn't put in the effort to figure out the ambiguity around Noah/Shem and Nahor/Terah). I suppose there's one other hiccup, depending on which particular version of the Bible you're using. Since we don't have an 'original' version of Genesis, we have to rely on copies of that version, most notably the Masoretic text and the Septuagint (though those aren't the only two). And those copies differ on certain details, including all those ages in Genesis 5 and Genesis 11. Exodus to Solomon's Temple Like I said, this one comes straight from a single verse, 1 Kings 6:1: In the four hundred eightieth year after the Israelites came out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv, which is the second month, he began to build the house of the Lord. Solomon's Temple to the Babylonian Captivity This is the period where things purportedly get a bit more complicated. I haven't gone through this period in detail, yet, myself, but to give just one example, you have this verse from 2 Kings 3:1: In the eighteenth year of King Jehoshaphat of Judah, Jehoram son of Ahab became king over Israel in Samaria; he reigned twelve years. Go through finding all those verses and work out the years, and you come up a little over 4 centuries of history. In a somewhat independent path, other books in the Bible also give more genealogies, such that you can trace each and every claimed descendant from Adam all the way to Jesus. Granted, there aren't ages associated with all of those genealogies, but these also give a ballpark range in the thousands of years. So, if you accept the claims of the Bible at more or less face value, and assume all those genealogies represent real people and not just imaginary people made up out of thin air, and that all the events in Egypt, Israel, and Judah all really happened, you'll end up at an estimate for the date of creation somewhere around 4000 BC. As a side note, while it seems to be somewhat fashionable to dismiss exercises like these because some parts of the Bible were ‘obviously’ meant to be taken more metaphorically or allegorically, I don’t see such figurative interpretations as obvious at all. The crux of this argument would be the genealogies in Genesis 5 and Genesis 11 – after that, you’re already into Egyptian pharaohs, so nothing that’s going to be a major difference from real history (at least as far as timelines). But these genealogies aren’t fables with moral lessons or some type of simplified explanation of complex concepts for a pre-scientific society. They’re boring, dry lists of ancestry. It’s about as close to a conventional history section as you’ll find in Genesis – the part least likely to be metaphorical or allegorical (though there’s certainly a reason to ‘invent’ such lists to provide legitimacy for the rulers of Israel and Judah). *As I already touched upon, that difference of only a few decades is using a specific version of the Bible, such as the Masoretic text or the Septuagint. The differences between those different versions can add up to a couple millennia, though still not anywhere near on the magnitude of real history.

How has technology changed our lives? Technology essentially made our species possible. It's so ingrained into human existence that we barely even think about the most basic forms of technology, but we wouldn't be here without it. One of the most basic technologies, controlled use of fire, goes back at least around 1 million years. That predates Homo sapiens. It was probably Homo erectus that first developed that technology. Purposely shaped stone tools go back even further – 3.3 million years. That's before our ancestors had even evolved into the Homo genus. Those tools were probably made by something like Australopithecus afarensis or Kenyanthropus platyops. ABOVE SOURCE: Oldest stone tools pre-date earliest humans If you look at humans compared to a lot of other animals, while we're not as physically pathetic as some hyperbolic documentaries try to make us out to be, we're still on the slow, weak side when un-armed. But those ancient technologies that our ancestors developed allowed them to hunt, defend themselves, cook food, etc. That in turn allowed our ancestors to develop large, calorie hungry brains, while compensating with smaller muscles that didn't need as much nutrition as some of our bulkier cousins (I'm looking at you, gorillas, with your 5 to 10k calorie per day food requirements – The Influence of Seasonal Frugivory on Nutrient and Energy Intake in Wild Western Gorillas). Without that level of already existing technology in our pre-human ancestors, our own evolution just wouldn't have happened. And while we might consider those ancient technologies to be primitive, that's only from our spoiled perspective with our amazing modern technologies. You can see some uses of technology and tools in other animals, but our pre-human ancestors were already developing technologies beyond what other animals were doing. And by the time actual humans developed, there was a whole plethora of technologies – basket weaving, ropes, clothing, spears, etc. And once agriculture developed around 10k years ago and people could begin accumulating more possessions than just what they could carry, technology really took off. So how has technology changed our lives? By making our very existence possible.

Isn't it crazy that 1 man managed to convince billions of people that they evolved from an animal? Actually, yes it is. That's why Darwin is held in such high esteem as the genius he was, and why he was granted the honor of being buried in Westminster Abbey. Other naturalists had proposed ideas of transubstantiation before Charles Darwin, including his grandfather Erasmus Darwin. However, none of those predecessors had managed to convince the larger scientific establishment to take evolution particularly seriously. And Edward Blyth had hit on ideas of natural selection before Darwin published the Origin, though Blyth's comments on the matter went largely unnoticed. Somewhat famously (at least among us nerds), William Wallace also discovered natural selection independently, and even submitted a joint presentation of papers with Darwin to the Linnaean Society of London in 1858. But this submission also didn't have much impact. What did have tremendous impact was when Darwin finally published his book, On the Origin of Species, in 1859. The arguments and evidence he compiled in that book were enormously compelling. Practically overnight, evolution and universal common descent went from a somewhat disreputable position among fringe academics to accepted mainstream science. It was a monumental work on par with the likes of Newton and Einstein. Much of science progresses by incremental contributions from many different researchers. The subsequent history of evolutionary science after Darwin does follow this more general pattern. Looking through the Wikipedia article on the Modern synthesis, you find plenty of contributors like Ernst Mayr, G. Ledyard Stebbins, Theodosius Dobzhansky, E. B. Ford, Bernhard Rensch, Ivan Schmalhausen, George Gaylord Simpson, R. A. Fisher, William Bateson, Julian Huxley, J.B.S. Haldane, and more. But none of those folks, as intelligent as they were, had the same paradigm shifting impact as Charles Darwin. To put it another way, human knowledge had finally progressed to the point where discovering evolution was practically inevitable. It would have happened eventually. But without Darwin, it would have been a more prolonged process that would have taken a bit longer, and the folks who contributed would probably still be mentioned in the history books, but they wouldn't be household names (just look to Alfred Wegener and continental drift). Darwin was a true genius, with a monumental impact on biology. So yes, it is always a bit crazy when you come across such singular geniuses.

When did the celebration of Christmas begin to shift away from its religious origins? Sadly, some time around the Middle Ages, or perhaps a bit later at the Protestant Reformation. Prior to that, the pagan religious origins of some Christmas celebrations were still in full swing, and let me tell you, they sound fun. To be clear, the source of Christmas traditions is a bit mixed. While certain Internet sources would have you believe that it's entirely based on pagan traditions, the truth is more nuanced. But that's not really what I want to write about in this answer, so here's a link, if you're interested: However, it is true that when Christmas was first getting started and Roman pagans were converting to Christianity, they brought over a lot of their old traditions with them, particularly traditions related to Saturnalia, since it was celebrated around the same time of year. And these were fairly rowdy traditions, more in line with Mardi Gras than spending quality time with the family by the fireplace. There were costumes, props, heavy drinking, singing, gambling, and a Lord of Misrule, where one commoner was elected by the people to be the temporary 'leader' for the day. I read one description of Christmas as “like a nightmarish cross between Halloween and a particularly violent, rowdy Mardi Gras." (source) Here's one of my favorite pictures of this Christmas tradition. You've got the whole rabble entering into the church to confront the clergy and nobleman to assert the Lord of Misrule’s leadership. And look at that assemblage. You've got the Lord of Misrule himself (they guy wearing the pointy cap), a jester, fake knights on fake horses, and even somebody dressed up like a dragon. ABOVE: The Abbot of Unreasons by Cruikshank SOURCE: Lord of Misrule - Wikipedia Here are a couple more of these illustrations that I like to get across the feel of ‘traditional’ Christmas celebrations. ABOVE: This one’s got a fish man, if you look close enough. SOURCE: Lord of Misrule ABOVE: Lots of interesting costumes SOURCE: Bodleian Library MS. Bodl. 264, pt. I Christmas caroling also grew out of this. It didn't start as a bunch of folks going around singing songs just to make people happy. The carols were more like drinking songs, and the carolers were demanding food and drink from the houses of the rick folks that they visited. You can see this in a few Christmas carols that people still sing, like We Wish You a Merry Christmas (in the verses where they demand the figgy pudding) or Here We Come a-Wassailing (i.e. everybody drinking alcohol out of the communal Waissail bowl). ABOVE: Everybody Getting Sloshed Off the Wassail Bowl SOURCE: The Centuries-Old History of Wassail - Tales of the Cocktail Foundation Starting in the Middle Ages, stodgy old holier-than-thou types tamped down on these traditions, probably simply because they didn’t want people to have fun, but justifying it by saying that they wanted to focus more on the Christian aspects of Christmas. So that’s when “Christmas begin to shift away from its [pagan] religious origins”. Anyway, now we’re left with a much more anodyne Christmas celebration. Oh sure, you might have the office Christmas party were somebody has a few too many Jack & Cokes. But nobody’s wandering around the neighborhood in drunken groups dressed up in costumes while demanding that their rich neighbors treat them to food and even more alcohol. But it still sounds like fun. Here are a few articles with more details on these traditional Christmas celebrations, if you’re interested:

What makes Google Maps superior to Apple Maps? One reason – north up maps. Maybe I'm just old fashioned from the old days of using paper maps*. But I really, really, really prefer maps to always be oriented as north up when I'm driving. I know it might not be the most intuitive when you need to make split second decisions. But in the long run, it gives you a much better perspective and sense of orientation. Especially when you're in an area where you might be spending some time and not just driving through once, it really helps you learn the area. I have a sense of the actual cardinal direction I'm heading, not just 'straight ahead'. I can see where neighborhoods lie in relation to each other. I can build up a mental map that corresponds to the map I see on the screen. In contrast, the maps that are constantly rotating to align with your direction of travel just completely destroy that sense of awareness and perspective. When I spent a few months in El Paso a couple years ago, I learned my way around much quicker thanks to Google Maps always keeping the map with north up. Otherwise, despite an ignominious beginning**, Apple Maps has grown into a decent app. It even seems to do better than Google Maps at some things, like telling you which lane to be in, and giving you more than one next step at a time. But until Apple decides to put in an option for users to keep the map oriented as north up even in guidance mode, I'm simply not going to use it. *I remember back when I was a kid, on road trip vacations, or when we first moved from Pennsylvania to Maryland, and I'd sit in the back seat of the car following along on a map to see where we were. Maybe it was all those years of practice that helps me follow along on north up maps, when so many other folks I know seem to get confused by it. **If you look at the other answers to this question, the ones trashing Apple Maps tend to be several years old.
