On what basis did evolutionists decide humans have a close common ancestry with apes, was it by looks? If so what about the kangaroo and the sloth? If by DNA, what about the banana? If it was by intelligence, what about the octopus? Carl Linnaeus is known as the father of modern taxonomy. He developed the now traditional system that you probably learned in high school biology – Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species. This system is a nested hierarchy that we now recognize as being due to evolutionary relatedness, but Linaeus himself was a creationist (he died before Darwin was even born), and was merely trying to recognize the pattern of God's creation. And he based his system largely on physical similarity. Of course, he went deeper than superficial resemblances, and looked at the entire anatomy of organisms. That is how, for example, he recognized that dolphins and whales were mammals and not fish. And Linnaeus recognized the obvious anatomical similarities between humans and other apes, putting humans, chimpanzees, and orangutans all in the same genus, Homo (gorillas weren't yet known to European naturalists, or he almost surely would have included them, as well). I mean, the similarities between humans and other apes is sometimes so striking it's almost eerie: ABOVE SOURCE: Bonobo photos by Frans de Waal Kangaroos and sloths aren't nearly so anatomically similar to humans as the other apes. I mean, yes they're both mammals, so they're more related to humans than, say, a magpie or an oak tree, but not at that same level of similarity as the other apes. I mean, kangaroos are marsupials, for heaven's sake, with many, may differences to us placental mammals. Linnaeus recognized this over 200 years ago. DNA wasn't recognized as our hereditary molecule until the 1940s, and it's only been in more recent decades that scientists have been able to sequence DNA and otherwise study it in much more detail. Much like the anatomical comparisons that Linnaeus pioneered, you can also compare the similarity of the DNA of different organisms, and construct nested hierarchies of similarity. And when scientists did this, the resulting 'trees' matched up nearly spot on with the trees developed from traditional classification. In other words, while we knew from anatomical comparisons that humans were more closely related to apes than to sloths, DNA studies found exactly the same thing. So you have two different lines of evidence to do these comparisons, yet they produce essentially the same results. You mentioned bananas. Bananas are only distantly related to us people, and the genetics confirms this. While our DNA is roughly 98% the same with chimpanzees (it depends on how exactly you're doing the comparison), it's only around 50% the same with bananas. But bananas are multicellular eukaryotes, so even they are more closely related to us than some other life forms. Bacteria, for example, are even more distant relatives, with even less DNA in common with us. Your last question is about intelligence. The thing about lots of evolutionary traits is that they can develop separately through convergent evolution. When this happens, although the traits might have superficial resemblance, there will be lots of differences in the details. And octopuses and other cephalopods have brains that are very different from us mammals. They developed their intelligence through a completely different evolutionary path than us. So yes, anatomical similarities and genetic similarities are both used to determine the relatedness of organisms. But intelligence is a trait that can evolve independently, so it’s not as useful on its own.

Can a jet break windows if it breaks the sound barrier far away from the building but then it flies by it? I think I see the misconception in the way you worded the question. A sonic boom isn't a one time event that occurs just at the instant an airplane surpasses the speed of sound. It's a shockwave that trails behind the aircraft the entire time it's flying faster than the speed of sound. When pressure waves move out away from an object, the wavefront is a sphere expanding at the speed of sound. That's basically what the speed of sound is, since sound is itself pressure waves in air. As long as you're below the speed of sound, those pressure waves can expand faster than the aircraft is moving. But once you hit the speed of sound, those pressure waves can't expand out faster than the aircraft is moving, so they pile up on the front side, creating a 'wall' of high pressure air known as a shock wave . As the aircraft flies even faster than the speed of sound, this shockwave trails behind the aircraft in the shape of a cone. This conic shockwave travels along with the aircraft. When it passes you by, that sudden increase in pressure is the sonic boom. So, it doesn't matter how long ago the aircraft first exceeded the speed of sound. It matters how fast it's going when it's flying over you. If it's supersonic, it will still be creating that shockwave, and you'll still experience the sonic boom as the shockwave passes you by. In reality, with all the different parts of an aircraft sticking out into the air, you'll have multiple shockwaves coming off of the aircraft. But with those shockwaves being so relatively close together, and the aircraft flying so fast, you'll experience them all combined as one event.

Having a new species require at least 2 mutated species (male and female) with same characteristics, and they need to be around the same area to have any chance of mating. If it is that difficult, how are there so many species on earth today? What you're referring to is saltationism (from the Latin term for jump), sometimes referred to a little more colorfully as the hopeful monster hypothesis. The idea was that large macromutations create new species in a single blow. But, as the colorful name and your question point out, how would such hopeful monsters find partners to mate with? This idea did have some proponents back in the late 1800s and early 1900s, but the incorporation of genetics into evolutionary theory and the Modern Synthesis caused the idea to be mostly abandoned, at least for sexually reproducing animals. Evolution is a gradual accumulation of genetic changes within an entire population. Populations already have genetic diversity. It's why no two individuals look exactly alike. And genetic mutation is decently common. In us humans, for example, it seems that pretty much everybody has a handful of new mutations*. But this genetic diversity doesn't keep us (or other populations of animals) from mating. And the new mutations that do creep into the population don't instantly create new species. They just add to the existing genetic diversity. For a population to split into two species takes time and isolation. The population somehow gets split into two separate populations, let's say Population A and Population B, that can't or don't mate with each other. These constant mutations will continue to spontaneously arise in each population, but they'll be limited to their respective populations. Mutations that arise in Population A, for example, can mix into that population over generations as all those animals mate with each other, but as long as Population B remains isolated from Population A, those mutations won't jump over to Population B. They'll be limited to Population A. And the same goes vice versa for new mutations that arise in Population B. Over time, as each of these population acquires more and more different mutations, they'll become more and more distinct from each other. Eventually, they'll have become different enough to be new species, but it's still a gradual process, with no stark dividing line. ABOVE SOURCE: Islands of speciation and speciation on islands This also explains why species is such a fuzzy boundary, with 'lumpers' and 'splitters' often disagreeing on whether different populations should be separate species, or merely subspecies. For example, a single study from 2020 , showed that there could be anywhere from 2 to 6 different species of giraffe depending on which specific criteria you used to define species. But sexually reproducing animals aren't the only organisms out there. Many types of animals are hermaphrodites, with male and female reproductive organs on the same individual. Many plants also produce male and female reproductive organs (stamens and pistils) on the same plant. If one of these types of organisms were to experience a substantial mutation, then it could potentially create a new species with that individual. In fact, this actually has been observed decently often for plants (take a look at section 5.1 of this page, Observed Instances of Speciation). Another exception is animals that reproduce by parthenogenesis, which is just a fancy term to describe animals where an egg can develop without being fertilized by a male. A notable recent case is the marbled crayfish. Their ancestral species is the slough crayfish from Georgia and Florida. People captured slough crayfish for pets, which led to captive breeding to supply the pet trade. Some time around the mid '90s, somebody in Germany discovered the new species, marbled crayfish, which can reproduce parthenogenetically. This new species like arose from a mutation in a single individual. (You might also see these animals referred to by their German name, marmokrebs.) So, your intuition was partially right about sexually reproducing animals. Even if there were massive mutations that would create a new species in a single individual, the odds of such mutations happening simultaneously to create a male and female of that new species are so astronomically low as to be effectively impossible. But, that’s not the way speciation actually occurs in sexually reproducing animals. It’s a gradual process among populations due the accumulation of many, many mutations. But among other types of organisms that can reproduce by themselves and so don’t have the problem of being hopeful monsters, then speciation can sometimes happen in a single individual. * The overall mutation rate is on the order of 100 - 200 mutations per person. But given that something like 90% of our genome is junk DNA, most of those mutations don't do much at all. Still, it seems that we do all get at least a handful of mutations to functional DNA. What is the atheist position on respect for other people's beliefs (especially religious ones)? The problem is that 'respect' has multiple meanings. Quoting Google, here are the three most relevant (for a verb, the meanings for a noun are similar): Nobody's beliefs are entitled to respect in that first sense merely for holding them. Not all beliefs are equal. Some people, for example, believe the earth is flat. That's not an admirable belief, at all, and in the sense of the first definition, I don't respect such beliefs. However, the second two definitions are much more in a sense of tolerance. You don't have to admire somebody's beliefs to respect their right to hold such beliefs. If someone wants to believe in a flat earth, that's their right, and I 'respect' that. Religious beliefs can vary quite widely, from Unitarian Universalists or Buddhists (who might actually be atheists) to Methodists to hard core young earth creationist Southern Baptists, and plenty of others. To reiterate what I already said, none of those beliefs are entitled to respect in that first sense merely for existing. If you want me to respect your beliefs in the sense of admiration, then those beliefs better be worthy of admiration. But religious beliefs that contradict reality, or that preach intolerance, definitely don't fit the bill. However, everybody has the right to believe whatever they want (within reason), even if it is something that I find rather silly or absurd. If you want to believe the entire universe was created just a few thousand years ago, that's your right. Where things start to get messy is when your beliefs harm others, or when you try to impose your beliefs on others, such as the recent and infamous draconian abortion laws in states like Texas. When your beliefs in opposition to abortion begin to affect other people, then there's an issue. You have the right to have such beliefs, but absent a compelling secular purpose, you shouldn't be able to force those beliefs on others. If someone doesn't want to consider abortion as an option for themselves, I respect that. If someone wants to take away that option for others, they've crossed a line. Per the third definition up above, tolerating such beliefs wouldn't actually be "avoid harming or interfering with" others, since those beliefs are doing that, already. So really, it depends on which particular sense of 'belief' your referring to, and which particular religious beliefs you're referring to. And depending on which combination, the answer can range from respecting certain beliefs, to not respecting other beliefs, to being vehemently opposed to yet others.

Why aren't autogyros as popular as cars? I'm not sure everyone knows exactly what an autogyro is, so let me start off with some background. Way back in the day, before practical helicopters, autogyros were the first practical rotorcraft. But unlike helicopters, the rotor isn't powered in flight. It's made to spin by aerodynamic means, technically known as autorotation. So, autogyros can't hover, and they still need a propeller or some other form of propulsion. Still, back in those early days, autogyros gave much better short field performance than airplanes, along with improved low speed handling characteristics (no stall since your ‘wings’ are rotating independently of your airspeed). As autogyro technology advanced, they even developed jump takeoff abilities, where a clutched driveshaft from the engine would spin up the rotor to a high rpm on the ground, and then increase the pitch on the blades and use that rotor inertia to jump into the air. The rotor head can still be simpler than a helicopter, and you also don’t need a tail rotor (no torque to the rotor once you’re in the air). Here’s a Pitcairn PA-36, towards the zenith of autogyro popularity before being eclipsed by helicopters, demonstrating jump takeoff and short landing capabilities: Nowadays, gyros are mostly relegated to small recreational aircraft, not quite as mechanically complex as that PA-36 up above. They split the difference between airplanes and helicopters, while remaining much less complex and less expensive than helicopters. I’ve seen ultralight gyros take off in the space of about 25 ft, and touch down vertically with no roll out. ABOVE: A typical modern recreational autogyro SOURCE: AutoGyro MT-03 - Wikipedia Anyway, on to the question of why autogyros aren't as popular as cars. First, personal aircraft in general, from airplanes to helicopters to autogyros, are never going to be as popular as cars. The training to become a pilot is more extensive and regulated than earning a driver's license. The extra rigor of aircraft certification and maintenance drives higher prices. Aircraft, even rotorcraft, can only fly between locations that can easily accommodate aircraft (i.e. no door to door from your house to the mall). And bad weather and high winds are a much bigger deal for air travel, and would ground the aircraft during storms or fog that are a mere nuisance in cars. In other words, you'll still need cars, so personal aircraft would be your second or third vehicle. As far as why autogyros are even less popular than airplanes and helicopters, it's because they fall somewhere in the middle performance-wise, so they don't perform typical rotorcraft missions as well as helicopters, or fixed-wing missions as well as airplanes. If you need to hover, you need a helicopter. And if you want to fly fast, airplanes are more efficient than most gyros. There are some companies trying to push modern day gyros if you only need short/zero roll takeoffs and landings but not full hover capability, but truth be told, the market hasn’t really embraced gyros very widely beyond personal / recreational vehicles. As an aside, there have been efforts over the years for even more advanced autogyros. Particularly well known (at least among aviation nerds) was the Fairey Rotodyne. They actually powered the rotor with tip jets for takeoff and landing, so it could hover. But then they transitioned the rotor to autorotation in flight, reducing the rpm to reduce drag and using the wings and props to fly more like an airplane. It's major drawback was that those tip jets were LOUD, though perhaps that might have been addressed had it not been for politics when Fairey was acquired by Westland Aircraft who already had a competing rotorcraft division. Anyway, it was still an interesting concept:

Why does my keyboard have a caps lock key? It must have some purpose, right? This is a good question. Is there really a need for a caps lock key on modern keyboards? How many times do most people use it intentionally, vs. eNDING UP WITH SENTENCES UNINTENTIONALLY WRITTEN IN ALL CAPS? The obvious function is that it lets you write in all caps, LIKE THIS, without having to hold down the shift key. This stems from old, mechanical typewriters, where the shift key actually did mechanically shift the typing mechanism to switch between lower case and upper case letters, which required a decent amount of force on the key. So, for prolonged all caps typing, a shift-lock locked the mechanism in the shifted position, easing the load on your pinky fingers. But shift-lock shifted all the keys, including the symbols on numbers, so a slightly later innovation was caps-lock that only shifted the letters, not the entire keyboard. Once electric typewriters, word processors, and early computers came around, the effort to hold down shift wasn’t nearly so hard, but it was still nice to have a caps-lock key. Remember that typewriters and early printers (like Daisy wheels) still didn’t allow for much formatting or different font sizes, so all-caps was still a convenient way to distinguish things like titles and headings. But on modern day computers? Just about any serious project that needs to be in all-caps can be handled by software, and in many cases, it’s even preferable to do it that way. For example, for headings in a paper, you should type them out in normal mixed case, e.g. Heading Example. Then, if you want it in all caps, just change the heading style to all caps, and the word processing software will take care of it for you. But if you decide later to switch back to mixed case, it’s just a quick change of the style rather than re-typing everything. In my own field, technical drawings use all caps as the standard for drawing annotations, but this can also be handled through software settings instead of using caps-lock (e.g. Displaying Annotation Notes in Uppercase). Even typing here on Quora, there are already a basic text formatting options. Adding an all-caps to that would be simple. There may be some niche applications, like programming, where caps-lock still has a bit of use, but I imagine a lot of that’s driven by complacency. Remove the caps-lock key from the keyboard, and programming software would pretty quickly include software features*. The more I think about it, the more I’d like to see the caps-lock key done away with, to free up that space on the keyboard for something more useful. Maybe replace it with a keyboard shortcut to enable all caps (like alt-shift-c), or at least relegate it to a far corner of the keyboard where you’re less likely to hit it by accident. Here’s something related I found doing a bit of googling: *I’m only a novice programmer, with most of my experience in Visual Basic (which just earned me several snorts of derision from the real programmers). But even back in VB 6, I only worried about capitalization when I declared my variables. After that, I typed them in all lower case, and VB would automatically convert them to the capitalization from when they were declared. Not only did it save me the effort of pressing the shift key, it was a nice, quick double check that I typed in the correct variable name (if it didn’t update capitalization, I’d made a typo).

If a Starship without any payload can barely reach up to orbital speeds while expending almost ALL of the fuel within it, then could it be that SpaceX underestimated how easy/difficulty would be conceiving a fully reusable craft? Look, I've got my reservations about SpaceX's approach to safety with their 'Let's just blow stuff up till it quits blowing up approach'*, and I think that they can sometimes be a bit overhyped by Musk fanbois.** But let's keep things in perspective. They're a company with tons of talent from professional aerospace engineers. Even if they underestimated the difficulty of this approach back in the very beginning, by the time you're building and testing full scale prototypes, you've already gone through feasibility studies, trade studies, preliminary design, detail design, and tons and tons of analysis. You either need prohibitive numbers of test flights, or you need to do lots and lots of traditional analysis. But if it takes half a dozen attempts to get even your first successful full flight, then your traditional analysis couldn't have been all that robust. On the other hand, other rocket manufacturers have plenty of failures, as well, so extreme risk in comparison to aviation just seems to be part of the game (though when Musk starts his dreaming about sending millions of people to Mars, that's when this safety approach becomes irresponsible). **In fairness, while Musk fanbois might overhype SpaceX, there are plenty of folks who go too far the other way, criticizing SpaceX too harshly merely because Musk himself seems to be a bit of a jackass. What was your initial reaction to learning about evolution in school? Did you immediately believe it or did you have doubts about its validity? It was a revelation. Prior to that, my exposure to evolution was pop-science articles or the way it was casually discussed in nature documentaries. And while those treat evolution as a given, and may even discuss evolutionary relationships, they hardly ever go into detail of the mechanisms or how evolution actually works. So, like many folks, I had a more Lamarckian view of evolution, of use and disuse and even intentionality on the parts of organisms. I remember one example in particular that left me dumbfounded, of a symbiotic relationship between certain plant and ant species, where the plants provided food and shelter for the ants in exchange for the ants protecting the plants. How could either one of them have intentionally initiated such a relationship? How could organisms with such little to no cognitive ability do anything intentional at all? ABOVE SOURCE: Ecological and Evolutionary Responses of Protective Ant-Plant Mutualisms to Environmental Changes (Chapter 11) - Ant-Plant Interactions When I was finally formally taught the mechanisms of mutation and natural selection, it all fell into place. You don't need any intention. Mutations are just mistakes on a mechanical level, so diversity is inevitable. And as soon as you have diversity, differential reproduction is also inevitable. Evolution didn't just make sense. There was simply no way it couldn't happen. Even my ant-plant example finally made sense. All you needed was some type of mutation on a plant to attract certain ants, and given ants' aggressive behaviors, that would protect the plants from other organisms that might try to eat them. And from there, additional mutations just refine the relationship further. So while I might have said that I already accepted evolution prior to my high school biology class, I didn't actually understand it. By learning how evolution actually works, that class made me much more certain in the truth of evolution. I still had a period of minor doubt a few years later when Intelligent Design was at its peak popularity, wondering if I was being a good Christian when so many other Christians insisted you had to accept some form of creationism. So I researched evolution even deeper than that high school biology class, and given that the evidence really is overwhelming, I only became more certain of evolution. (I might add, that while it's certainly possible to be a Christian and accept evolution, this incident was one of the stimuli to start me on the path to atheism.)

If you don’t reach escape velocity, but with as much fuel as you need, would you be able to leave Earth? There are a several things to understand here. First is what escape velocity actually means. It's the velocity you would have to be moving, that without any more thrust (i.e. just coasting from then on out) that you would be on a path to eventually 'escape' Earth's gravity (or whatever other body you're talking about escaping, such as the Sun, the Moon, or other planets). Next, escape velocity is dependent on your distance from the Earth (or whatever other body), since the influence of Earth's gravity decreases the further away you get. At the surface, escape velocity is 25k mph (40k km/h). But as you get further away from Earth, the escape velocity drops pretty rapidly at first, and then slowly begins approaching zero. But another big consideration is something known as the sphere of influence (or the related Hill sphere). While it's technically true that gravity from the Earth extends to an infinite distance, there are so many other bodies in our own solar system and broader universe, that at a relatively 'minor' distance (in astronomical terms, at least), the Earth's gravity becomes negligible compared to other bodies. Within our solar system, for example, the Earth's sphere of influence (per Wikipedia) is 577k miles (929k km), which is roughly 2.4x further away than the Moon orbits the Earth. Once you get further than that from the Earth, the Sun's gravity will overwhelm the Earth's, and an object's motion will be governed almost entirely by the Sun's gravity (assuming it's not within some other planet or moon's sphere of influence). So, if you were thinking of escape velocity as 25k mph, realize that that's only close to the surface of the Earth. If you had some means to continuously provide thrust and continuously move away from Earth, eventually you would get far enough away that whatever speed you were moving would be greater than the Earth's escape velocity at that distance – it will just be a lot lower than that 25k mph at the surface. Or, if you were to travel far enough that you went past the Earth's sphere of influence, then the Earth's gravity would be negligible compared to the Sun's, and your path would instead be dominated by the Sun's gravity. (And of course, if you could somehow keep moving away from the Sun, you would eventually get far enough away that the Sun's gravity would be negligible compared to the overall galaxy.) The kicker, though, is how you would actually accomplish that continuous thrust, and just exactly what you mean by "with as much fuel as you need". Rockets already are designed to get the most bang for the buck out of the fuel they can carry. They accelerate so quickly because it is the best way to do it. Consider the extreme – imagine if you had a rocket that generated just enough thrust to hover*. You'd sit there burning fuel, but not climbing. You'd eventually run out of fuel without going anywhere, no matter how much fuel you carried. If you barely increased your thrust, you'd climb slowly, but you'd still run out of fuel before you made it very far. And it's not simply a matter of carrying more fuel. That extra fuel is going to make you heavier, which means you'll need even more thrust, burning more fuel, in a vicious cycle of diminishing returns. You really need to read up on the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation if you want to understand this mathematically, but the best use of your fuel is to accelerate as quickly as possible. As long as we're stuck using rockets, slow, leisurely climbs just aren't a realistic possibility to get into space. *Of course, this thought experiment is still simplifying things, since your rocket will get lighter as it burns off fuel. But I suppose you could be using rocket engines that could be throttled, so that you can constantly adjust the thrust to that required for hover.

If could put a space plane in a 100km high orbit, would the small amount of lift move it in to a higher orbit? Look at it this way. If you had a normal plane at a normal altitude and cut the engines, do you think the plane will start going higher because of the lift? No. Because airplanes also have drag, and that drag will rob the aircraft of energy. Without the thrust from the engines, the only way to maintain speed is to use gravity to descend. If a space plane were in orbit to where there was enough atmosphere to create a non-negligible amount of lift, it would also create a non-negligible amount of drag. That drag would begin to slow the space plane down. That in itself would be enough to make the plane begin losing altitude because of the way orbits work (you’re always falling, it’s just that your horizontal velocity keeps you moving sideways fast enough that you keep on ‘missing’ the ground). If you did want to maintain your speed without using engines, you’d have to descend even faster.

Why do we, as atheists, like shows that depict religion as fact? Doesn't that make us hypocrites? You’re basically just asking why people like fantasy. It could be wizards and wands like Harry Potter, orcs and rings like The Lord of the Rings, Greek gods and goddesses like Percy Jackson, or angels and the Christian God like The Golden Compass. Heck, if you’re into books that are so bad they’re, well, not good, but at least amusing, you can even read the Left Behind series. You can suspend disbelief and enjoy fantasy without that counting as some sort of endorsement that you think the fantasy world is real. There’s nothing hypocritical about that.

So I may be saying some minor spoilers, here, but the plot of the movie revolved around Bella, a Frankenstein-esque creation of a newborn's brain transplanted into an adult's body. She had matured into basically the mental age of a toddler for the bulk of the movie. But with the anatomy of an adult, this toddler discovered the pleasures of sexual arousal, and went around experimenting with this newfound activity. And the main antagonist of the movie spent enough time with Bella, that even if he didn't know her full history, it was clear that she wasn't the mental equivalent of a normal adult. The cutesy euphemism of ‘furious jumping’ just drove home Bella’s immaturity. The whole thing was very difficult to watch. Feifei Wang has already written a very good review of the movie that I'd recommend reading in full: As she notes, this movies leans very heavily into the 'born sexy yesterday' trope, which is problematic enough just about any time it's used. But in my opinion, this is one of the ickiest examples of the trope I've seen, since it was an actual human toddler's brain, not some exotic alien or magical creature that you could at least try to chalk up to not being human. Here's an excerpt from Ms. Wang's answer that I think makes an excellent point: Secondly, why sex? Could Bella experience and explore the world some other way? Did Frankenstain’s monster go on a sex escapade after he escaped Victor’s lab? No. He went to learn about the world like a fucking normal person. Why did Bella go out to see the world, and all we (as audiences) saw were the various men she had sex with in bed? Why does Gen Z want to get rid of the electoral college? Do they really want liberal California and New York deciding the outcome of presidential and federal elections for the entire country? This isn't a Gen Z thing. It goes back many decades. Here are results from polling by Gallup going back to the 1960s: ABOVE SOURCE: Americans Would Swap Electoral College for Popular Vote As you can see, in 1969, there was overwhelming public support for a Constitutional amendment for direct election of the president. Here are some more recent results from Pew: ABOVE SOURCE: By about 2 to 1, Americans want popular vote, not Electoral College, to decide who is president Things got a bit close in 2017, but the majority of the country has still favored the popular vote to elect the President over that entire time. Support for the popular vote is on a bit of an upswing right now, but it's still not as high as it was back in 1969. So yeah, it's far from a Gen Z phenomenon. I myself support the popular vote for the President. I was starting to type up a long explanation, but it really just comes down to wanting every person to have an equal say in who's the President, because that’s what a fair democracy looks like. Right now, depending on whether you're in a big state, a small state, a solid red state, a solid blue state, or a swing state, they all have an effect on how much of a difference your individual vote makes. But why? Why should where I live make a difference in the impact of my vote? I’ve lived in 3 different states so far. Why does my impact on the Presidential election change each time I move to take a new job? I want my vote for the President to have the same impact no matter what state I might live in. And the only fair thing is for everybody else's vote to have the same impact.

For Atheists, who is Jesus to you, given historical evidence of his existence? Which Jesus are we talking about? The Jesus of the Gospels, or the historical Jesus without all the myth and legend tacked on? By way of example, consider Saint Nicholas vs. Santa Claus. Santa Claus may be based on a real, historical Saint Nicholas, but the legend has diverged so far from reality in all that time, that the characters contain very little in common. What's more, we don't actually know all that much about the real Saint Nicholas, so it's tough to say too much about him. That's the same way it is for the historical Jesus vs. the Gospel Jesus. The historical Jesus probably existed, but there's just very little in the way of reliable evidence on what he might have been like. Paul's authentic letters are some of the earliest mentions we have of Jesus, but they don't contain much in the way of biographical details. The Gospels are much more detailed, but also come from decades later, and were almost certainly second hand accounts spread by word of mouth before educated Christians finally committed them to paper. Considering how quickly urban legends can pop up in the modern day, and how often we see misattributed quotes (Mark Twain didn't say nearly so much as the Internet memes claim he did), a decades long gap is a lot of time for the legends around Jesus to grow and morph. So it's really tough to say much of anything about the historical Jesus – whether he was an honest preacher whose image got embellished over the years, a conman who intentionally mislead people with lies and sleight of hand tricks to build a reputation as a miracle worker, a bit of a crazy religious zealot who might have believed a lot of what he said, or just about anything else you can imagine. We've got plenty of modern day religious figures as examples for any of those scenarios. As far as the more legendary Jesus of the Gospels, as I've said before, my opinion is a bit mixed. Everyone is plenty familiar with the good things he said (feed the poor, love your neighbor, don't judge others, etc.), so there's no need for me to repeat all that here. But he also had plenty of more troubling teachings. Since I've already written about this before (Jeff Lewis's answer to Being an atheist, I know you do not believe in God, but do you see Jesus (the character) as being a good role model? Why?), I'm going to quote that here: But let's not forget who the historical Jesus was – a religious extremist and a cult leader. He supposedly told his followers things like, "Whoever is not with me is against me," and "Whoever comes to me and does not hate father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, yes, and even life itself, cannot be my disciple." If a Jim Jones, David Koresh, or L. Ron Hubbard were to say such things we'd call them out as gigantic red flags. Just because Christianity went on to become a major religion doesn't mean it was okay when (if) Jesus said those things in the first place. Although Christians were quick to rationalize/accommodate Jesus's failed prophecies, he himself seemed to believe that the coming age of the Son of Man was imminent, "Truly I tell you, there are some standing here who will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom." That, and his belief that God would take care of people with enough faith, led to several teachings that are rather irresponsible if you actually have to plan for the future. "Therefore do not worry, saying, ‘What will we eat?’ or ‘What will we drink?’ or ‘What will we wear?’ For it is the Gentiles who strive for all these things; and indeed your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things." Or his admonition to the rich young man, "If you wish to be perfect, go, sell your possessions, and give the money to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me." At times, Jesus also had a bit of a black & white way of looking at the world that lacked subtlety or nuance. One that's bothered me for a while is the way he equated temptation to actually acting on it. Consider his teaching on lust, "But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lust has already committed adultery with her in his heart." Seriously, ask any married person if they'd be as upset at their spouse for a momentary feeling of lust, or actually committing adultery. This type of teaching just sets people up for failure. Instead of framing it as a positive that someone was able to overcome their temptations, it berates people for having normal, natural emotions in the first place. [Going even further, you could frame that as adultery being no worse than lust, so if you've already lusted after somebody, you're not doing anything worse by actually carrying trough with action.] Then there's the whole episode with the money changers in the temple, which very well may have been the incident that led to his crucifixion. Now, it's one thing to have strong principles and to stand up for them. But it's another thing altogether to go onto somebody else's property to cause a major disturbance, vandalize the premises, and assault the people there. I mean, I can think of one church in particular here in my own town that I don't like, but I'm not going to show up there on a Sunday morning, smash up their altar, and start chasing people out of the pews. That's not how mature, sensible people handle disagreements. Finally, this last one may be a little unfair to the historical Jesus, since it comes from one of the stories that arose after his death, but I've always hated the doubting Thomas story. "Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe." No, no, no. It is not a virtue to believe things without evidence. It's this type of gullibility and naivety that leads people to give all their money to Nigerian princesses. Critical thinking and skepticism (not to be confused with cynicism) are skillsets that should be nurtured and celebrated, not discouraged. So, it's tough to say anything about the historical Jesus, because we just don't have much reliable evidence to know what he was really like. The Jesus of the Gospels was a mixed bag, with some good teachings, but plenty of troubling ones. Related:

If atheists begin to believe in my god, what would they lose? They will not lose anything. Your god must be the least demanding one out there, because a lot of the gods people believe in aren’t so laid back. For many Christians, there's the 10% tithe right off the bat. Back when I was still religious and my wife and I were looking for a church in town, one actually wanted to see our pay stubs so that they knew how much to extort from us each week. Sorry – I mean, how much we would 'donate'. Then there's the time investment. That's at least a couple hours every Sunday when I could be doing something else. Then there are lost opportunities. Muslims and Jews, for example, would deprive me of bacon cheeseburgers. Hinduism, Jainism, Buddhism, and Sikhism would deprive me of meat entirely. Southern Baptists would have me abstain from alcohol. Mormons would take that even further and have me abstain from even coffee and Diet Coke. Then you get into more serious issues like abortion rights for women, marriage equality and other civil rights for LGBTQ+ folks, Catholics' weird hang-ups against condoms which has exacerbated the HIV crisis in Africa, and on and on. And although I don’t want to discuss supernatural aspects too much since I don’t believe in any of them, what if you’ve picked the wrong god to believe in? If you want me to be a Christian but the ancient Egyptians were right, then I won’t know any of the spells to guide me to Field of Reeds. If the ancient Greeks were right, where would I get my coins to cross the River Styx? If Hindus are right, then following some of the more hateful forms of Christianity might screw up my karma and yield me a pretty bad life in my next reincarnation. I know, not every religion has every one of these issues. But there are plenty of costs and negative impacts that can come from certain specific religions. And when you look at that in comparison to the likelihood of Bronze Age to Iron Age mythology actually being true, well, I'm not going to lose any sleep over ordering a bacon cheeseburger and a pint at a bar in the middle of a pride rally.

Do you think there is a unique atheist approach to morality, or do atheists simply adhere to the same moral code as everyone else? I'd actually put it the other way around. I think that religious folks, despite often paying lip service to their religion or taking a few superficial rules from their scriptures, actually develop their moral code the same way as everyone else. Do you really need the Bible telling you that murder is wrong to avoid wanting to kill people? I don't mean in a 'ha-ha' hyperbolic sort of way, but the thought of literally taking somebody's life and living with that on your conscience. For most people, being averse to murder is just a part of human nature, independent of whatever religion they were raised in or lack thereof. On the other hand, do you agree that it's immoral to sell your daughter into slavery? Or simply to own slaves in general? Probably, even though the Bible says those things are perfectly fine. It merely sets some rules around those practices to keep them from becoming excessively bad, but even the New Testament has a passage instructing slaves to be loyal to their masters - 1 Peter 2:18. So, where do people get morality? It's a combination of innate instincts and human nature in things like empathy and fairness, built upon by social mores that we learn as we grow up, and perhaps even a bit of philosophy for the people who think about it a lot. If you're raised in a religious community, you may acquire the specific social mores of that community, but it's still the same general process as folks outside that community.

Can a Republican ever win the presidency again without some kind of a reset? Anyone remember headlines like these from 2008, when Obama had a strong victory and Democrats won a majority in the House and a supermajority in the Senate? Well, it only took until 2010 for the Republicans to win back control of the House, which they held onto for 8 more years until the 2018 election. And while Obama did manage to win re-election in 2012, I think we all remember what happened in 2016. And even in 2020, Trump only lost thanks to about 40 thousand voters in 3 key swing states. Even this year, 538 is currently giving Trump a 40% chance of winning the election, which is barely worse than a coin toss. That's just the nature of our two party system and polarized politics. The Democratic and Republican candidates will always get roughly half the vote. And with the way the electoral college currently biases the results towards rural states that tend to favor Republicans, presidential elections in particular will remain competitive, even when Democrats might have a nationwide advantage in raw numbers. So yes, the Republicans still have a very good chance of winning the presidency even maintaining their current strategies. They have a very good chance of winning this year. So don't get complacent like 2016, thinking a Democratic victory is a sure thing. Everybody needs to get out and vote to make sure their voice is heard.

Will electric kettles ever catch on in America? I think we’re all guilty of the occasional spontaneous purchase of at least a few kitchen gadgets. And I have to admit, we’ve got one of these electric kettles taking up cabinet space in our kitchen. My wife bought it during an extended stay at a hotel when she was working a contract, thinking the kettle would be useful in the confines of a hotel room when she otherwise only had a microwave and hot plate in her kitchenette. The times I stayed with her, we hardly ever used it. I mean, what’s the point? Nearly anything you cook needs to simmer for a while, not just take a one time hit of boiling water. And for the few times a year you do need hot water on its own (i.e. cup o’ noodle or hot chocolate), we’ve already got microwaves and stovetops. It’s not worth digging the electric kettle out of storage. And I’m not going to leave the kettle out all the time when it gets used so rarely in the first place. Plus, we have a Keurig coffe maker which already dispenses 4–12 oz of hot water on demand. It might not be quite boiling hot, but it’s good enough for hot chocolate. So although we own an electric kettle, I’m not at all surprised that they’re not more popular here in the U.S. They’re just one more kitchen gadget taking up shelf space, for a task that’s already accomplished by at least three other tools in the kitchen.

If tiktaalik evolved into acanthostega, why are there no intermediary forms? Why are there no intermediary forms between any two creatures that one evolved from? This reminds me of an old joke. A creationist complains to a scientist about a gap in the fossil record between an ancient animal and a modern one. The scientist gets lucky and finds a transitional form intermediate between the two. But the creationist just replies, 'Well now you've made the problem even worse. Instead of only one gap, now you have two.' Tiktaalik was only discovered in 2004. At the time, it was heralded as a near-perfect transitional form between fish like Panderichthyes and Eushthenopteron and early tetrapods like Acanthostega and Ichthyostega, and even acquired the nickname of being a 'fishibian'. It seems it didn't take long for creationists to now see two gaps instead of just one. But to actually answer the question, the reason is because fossils are quite rare. When most organisms die, their remains are completely consumed by scavengers and decomposers. It takes a very unique and unlikely set of circumstances to preserve their remains and go through the fossilization process. And then it takes another fortuitous set of circumstances for those fossils to be exposed through erosion, and then found before erosion carries on further and destroys them completely. The fossils we've found only represent a small subset of all the life that has ever existed on this planet. Just for perspective, consider the non-bird dinosaurs. We've only found something like 700 – 1000 non-bird dinosaurs species from their entire 165 million year history. In comparison, there are 6500 named mammal species just in the present, not counting unnamed living species, or the many, many species that have existed in the past and are now extinct. So we know that the actual number of dinosaur species over that entire 165 million year history must have been orders of magnitude higher than the mere 1000 species we've found so far. And it's the same for other groups of organisms. We know that the fossil record is largely incomplete, especially the fossils we've found so far. Some transitions are extremely well documented (like older apes to modern humans). Some remain pretty much entirely undiscovered (like non-flying animals to pterosaurs). But most fall somewhere in between (like fish to tetrapods). As researchers make more and more discoveries, they continue to fill in the gaps in our understanding. And for the time being, at least, this process shows no signs of slowing down. But even though we'll probably never know all of the details, everything we have found points squarely to natural evolutionary processes. Just as a side note, given how incomplete the fossil record is, it's very unlikely that we've found direct ancestor to descendant relationships in most cases. The transitional forms are more like cousins of the actual ancestors. In some cases, we know that certain fossils can't be ancestors because of the timeframes, but that instead they've preserved certain ancestral conditions.

What are the scientific odds of human existence? What conditions are necessary for life to exist? That's a very interesting question (the first one). The late Stephen Jay Gould came up with a thought experiment of 'rewinding' the history of life and starting over. Would you get the same results? How much of evolution is driven by randomness and chance, how much is driven by contingency, and how much is driven by more general principles? Here's how Gould himself put it: Suppose that ten of a hundred designs will survive and diversify. If the ten survivors are predictable by superiority of anatomy (Interpretation 1), then they will win each time – and Burgess eliminations do not challenge our comforting view of life. But if the ten survivors are protégés of Lady Luck or fortunate beneficiaries of odd historical contingencies (Interpretation 2), then each replay of the tape will yield a different set of survivors and a radically different history. And if you recall from high-school algebra how to calculate permutations and combinations, you will realize that the total number of combinations for 10 items from a pool of 100 yields more than 17 trillion potential outcomes. There's one particular experiment that comes as close as I can think of to replaying the tape of life, in the small scale, at least*. Back in 1988, Richard Lenski started out with one strain of E. coli, and split it into 12 different populations. He grew each population in identical conditions (well, as close to identical as experimentally possible) which were actually somewhat harsh for E. coli. He used a particular growth medium named DM25, which has a limited amount of glucose that the E. coli need to feed on. Lenski wanted to see how the E. coli would evolve due to this limited food supply. Every day, he would transfer 1% of the previous day's populations to new flasks with a fresh supply of DM25, periodically freezing samples to maintain as a kind of 'fossil record', and also periodically measuring attributes of the populations to see how they were evolving. The experiment is still ongoing today, making it one of the longest running (and supremely well documented) evolutionary experiments. Here's how one particular trait evolved in each of these populations, cell size: ABOVE SOURCE: E. coli long-term evolution experiment - Wikipedia While there's a general trend of increasing cell size in all 12 populations, they didn't all follow the exact same trend. In fact, the largest lineage evolved to be nearly twice as big as the smallest lineage. One particular adaptation was so rare that it only occurred in one of Lenski's populations.* The DM25 growth medium also happened to contain a large amount of citrate, which E. coli usually can't digest in anaerobic conditions, but which was included in the DM25 formulation way back when it was first developed for antibiotic experiments because it improved the efficiency of penicillin. Well, in this single lineage of Lenski's twelve E. coli populations, they did evolve the ability to digest citrate in anaerobic conditions. This adaptation is so profound for E. coli that some have proposed it actually represents a new species. So, starting from identical genetics, and subjecting populations to as identical of conditions as experimentally possible, each of the 12 populations took their own different evolutionary paths, from cell size, to the ability to digest citrate, to other traits I didn't mention here. There wasn't simply one optimum set of adaptations that natural selection drove towards in each population. This really does seem to indicate that chance† and contingency are major factors in the evolution of populations. And Lenski's experiment only had 12 isolated populations. What if he'd had 100? Would there be 100 unique strains by now? What about 1000? Or a million? Or to put it into the terminology of this question, what are the scientific odds of any particular strain of E. coli evolving in any particular flask? Based on Lenski's experiment, we can say it's no greater than 1 out of 12, but the reality could be a much, much smaller probability. So, let that play out in every population that's ever existed, and it seems that every particular species has a very low probability of existing‡. That goes for everything from ocelots to dandelions to Humboldt's squid to portabella mushrooms. And yes, it goes for us humans, as well. To add one more thing, it does seem like some body plans or adaptations are more common than others, implying that there are general principles that drive these adaptations. Levers to propel an organism on the seafloor or land, aka legs, have evolved in animals as diverse as insects, tetrapods, and starfish. Free swimming organisms evolved streamlined hydrodynamic bodies. Flying animals evolve wings. Etc. But other adaptations appear to be quite rare, like Lenski's citrate digesting E. coli. If elephants were to go extinct, I'm not sure we'd ever see another animal with that kind of trunk. And I can only hope that when aye-ayes go extinct, that particular combination of nightmare fuel never reappears. I rather suspect that we humans are kind of like elephants in that respect. You simply don't see many other animals similar to us outside our closest evolutionary cousins. We have a weird combination of an upright bipedal posture, complex social groups, extremely high intelligence with a penchant for technology combined with hands that are really good at manipulating our environments to effect that technology, along with several other unique characteristics. So, outside the general principle of all particular species being highly improbable, I'd say that even a species along the lines of us humans is highly improbable. Play the tape of life 1000 times, and while you might get lots of critters superficially resembling a crab, you might not get another elephant or another human. While I'm not sure anybody can give the precise odds, I think it's safe to say that the odds of human existence were quite low. So much of evolution is driven by chance and contingency, and we seem to be a rather odd combination of traits on top of that. That's all the more reason we need to get our acts together and make sure we don't screw up our planet (whether through things like climate change or good old fashioned global thermonuclear war). Because if we do go extinct, the odds are decent that nothing with our ability for science and understanding will ever evolve on this planet, again. *Both of these paragraphs are mostly copied from a previous answer of mine: †Chance could be things like Genetic drift or even the raw material of random mutation. ‡Don't confuse low probabilities of a particular species with low probabilities of life in general. A common analogy is shuffling a deck of cards. With 52 unique cards, the odds of any particular order for an entire deck is 1 in 10^68, an astronomically tiny probability. But, you're essentially guaranteed some order of 52 cards. That's the way it is with evolution and species – the odds of any particular species may be infinitesimally small, but the evolution of species in general is pretty much guaranteed. Argh. Once again, I failed to ensure I was answering an actual human before typing up my answer. You got me again, QPG. Oh well, I guess that means that at least some QPG questions aren’t trash.

Is reheating leftovers in a microwave good or bad? It depends on the food and your own taste buds. For me, they're fine for 'wet' foods, like mashed potatoes, macaroni and cheese, soups, etc. They're not so great for foods that need a crunchy or dry texture, like the breading on fried chicken, or the crust of a pizza. Microwaves tend to make such foods soggy, and, in my opinion, worse than just eating those foods cold. If you feel the need to reheat foods like that, you're better off using an oven, convection oven, or stovetop. If you're somehow worried about health risks because microwaves emit electromagnetic radiation, just remember that a light bulb also emits electromagnetic radiation. Microwaves are just a longer wavelength than visible light, which works out better for penetrating a bit more beneath the surface of food to excite the water molecules to heat them up. But a sufficiently powerful light bulb (or better yet, a heat lamp) will also heat up food just from visible light. Microwaves are no more dangerous to your food than shining a flashlight onto it or eating food in broad daylight. ABOVE: Microwaves are actually lower energy waves than visible light. It's the other end of the electromagnetic spectrum, with x-rays and gamma rays, where you have to worry about ionizing radiation SOURCE: Electromagnetic Spectrum - Introduction So, for the right kinds of food, microwaves do just fine for re-heating.

If Christianity is wrong, then why do people believe in it? Before getting into the why, let's get a little perspective. Here is the breakdown of global religious affiliation: SOURCE: The Changing Global Religious Landscape That's a lot of diversity of religions, and none of them are believed by a majority of the world's population. And since many of these religions are mutually contradictory, it stands to reason that most of them are wrong. So, your question isn't just applicable to Christianity. It's applicable to all religions. Why do people believe them, when logically, most of them must be wrong? A big reason is the cognitive bias that Deborah Kelemen has coined 'promiscuous teleology', which is a tendency to see purpose and intention even when it's not really there. Here's an explanation from one paper on the topic, Teleology and the intentions of supernatural agents: Given that according to PT [promiscuous teleology], teleological reasoning develops from an early understanding of intentionality which is then overextended (Kelemen, 1999a), the notion of agency is central to teleology. This is because the only things capable of having intentions are things with minds, and the only things with minds are agents. In this view, just as “chairs are for sitting on” is true only if an agent intends the chair to serve this function, the statement “clouds rain so that plants can grow” is based in the misbelief that plants growing is the intended function of the cloud raining. The difference between these two teleological explanations is that whereas the former implies the intentions of a natural agent (a human), the latter seems to imply the intentions of a supernatural agent. And here's the abstract from a different paper, Promiscuous Teleology: From Childhood Through Adulthood and from West to East: From infancy we continually try to make sense of what goes on around us. One strategy in making sense of things is to look for how things might be purposeful or designed. So useful is this strategy that sometimes it gets overused—what Deborah Keleman calls promiscuous teleology . This chapter reviews research with children and adults across cultures—including recent work in China —that demonstrates that promiscuous teleology is a conceptual default that all peoples share but that may be tamped down through enculturation. Kelemen argues that this teleological reasoning makes certain religious ideas about supernatural agents’ activity in creating or ordering the world largely intuitive. Or to summarize all that, our tendency to see agency everywhere makes us prone to supernatural explanations. Now, there are further questions as to why we might have evolved this cognitive bias in the first place. As I noted in another answer, "There are various explanations for why we might have evolved this bias – from being social animals and having to understand intentions of our fellow humans, to being prodigious tool makers and having an instinctual sense of 'function' for items. And there's no reason the explanations need to be mutually exclusive. (And even all that is assuming it's an adaptive trait, and not just a spandrel of San Marco.)" Add in how children credulously accept lessons from their parents (and understandably so – there's too much knowledge to pass down any other way), and culture, and how these stories morph and change over the generations, and you've got the perfect recipe for a large diversity of supernatural stories to explain various aspects of our world. Christianity just happens to be one of these myths among many.

Why is there so much debate over the math question 12÷2(2+4) =? A few other answers have said it's because the expression is ambiguous. But that's not really it. The expression isn't ambiguous at all. As an engineer myself, there's only one way to interpret that expression correctly. No. The issue is that lots of folks' exposure to math doesn't go much if at all beyond the high school level, and simplistic understandings of order of operations like PEMDAS or BODMAS. They don't know any further conventions that affect order of operations. The thing that makes this expression completely unambiguous is that there's no symbol in between the 2 and the parenthesis. That makes it clear that 2(2+4) is a single unit that can't be broken up. So the only appropriate way to interpret this expression is: 12 2 ( 2 + 4 ) What might have made this expression a bit ambiguous would have been to add a multiplication symbol: 12÷2×(2+4) Then it could be conceivable to interpret it a bit differently, perhaps instead as: 12 2 ( 2 + 4 ) However, even then, many engineers might interpret it the first way, keeping 2×(2+4) as a single unit as the denominator of the fraction. The reason is that when you're writing math 'inline' as opposed to formatting it the way math should really be written, division symbols are often treated as the fraction bar, with everything to the left assumed to be the numerator, and everything to the right assumed to be the denominator, and not cluttering things up with parentheses. As just one example, here are the definitions of some coefficients from one of my own engineering books, which I can assure you follow the convention that I just described (“my own” is in I own it, not that I wrote it). Really, if you wanted it to be 12/2, you'd probably put the parentheses around that to make it clear that 12/2 was a fraction, and instead write something like: (12/2)(2+4) But just to summarize, the expression as written in the original question isn't ambiguous. The issue is that lots of folks with only limited exposure to math don't know all the conventions affecting order of operations. And if there ever are any questions about ambiguity in an expression you’re writing, don’t be afraid to use parentheses.

How was the 2024 solar eclipse? Was there much of a panic/emergency as the USA prepared for or just a fizzle? The thing about preparing for potential emergencies, is that if you do your job well and avoid any problems, then everybody wonders what the fuss was about in the first place. The legitimate concerns around this eclipse (outside the conspiracy theories on Facebook) were mainly centered around so many people coming together in one area – things like traffic jams or strains on the supply chain (particularly food and fuel). Such concerns were based off the prior experiences of the 2017 eclipse. A report on traffic conditions, for example (TR News - Traffic Impacts of the 2017 Solar Eclipse), found that at least 5 million people had traveled to view that eclipse, that nearly all the Interstate highways in the path of totality ended up red on Google Maps immediately after the eclipse, and that some trips that would normally only take 4 hours by car actually took 13 hours in the wake of the eclipse. So, in preparation, some locations pre-emptively declared a state of emergency to be better able to address such concerns, or to be able to mobilize the National Guard for extra manpower just in case they would be needed, or made sure that highway related positions were all fully manned (e.g. toll booths, rest stops, emergency vehicles, etc.). Traffic did still turn out pretty bad in some places (there’s only so much you can do without changing the infrastructure), but I haven't heard of any major incidents or problems. So were officials over-prepared? Or did they just do a good job and help curtail any problems before they happened?

What is the science behind a ouija board? Has anyone ever had an experience that made them question reality? Ouija boards rely on a phenomenon know as the ideomotor effect. Here's how it's described in the article, What's The Spooky Science Behind The Ouija Board?: Basically, the ideomotor effect is subconscious, involuntary movement; scientists first documented it in 1852. "You often accidentally move a little bit if you think about a movement," says Marc Andersen, an assistant professor at the Interacting Minds Centre at Denmark's Aarhus University. "If you think about kissing your partner, for instance, you're inclined to just lean a little bit forward without really thinking about it." The same force is at work with Ouija boards: Participants think about the planchette moving, so they subconsciously move it themselves. But the movement of the planchette is only part of the Ouija board's mystery. What about the message? Our subconscious minds are responsible for those too. "Once it starts to spell something, inevitably, you're trying to guess, even if you're not doing it consciously," says [Chris] French. "If you ask, 'What's your name?' and it goes to the letter p, and then e, you're automatically thinking 'Peter.' Probably everybody else around the board is also thinking 'Peter.' And that's what is likely to be then spelt out." There have been multiple studies on people using Ouija boards, and probably unsurprisingly, it comes down to the vision of the people using the planchette. In one study by Dr. Andersen (from the quote above), participants wore goggles to track their eye movements. In a control case, when asked to spell out BALTIMORE, the participants all looked at each of the letters before moving the planchette there. If you only had the eye tracking data, you could have easily predicted that they were spelling BALTIMORE. When they went to open ended questions more typical of Ouija board use, at least one person in the group looked at each letter of the word that was eventually spelled out. In fact, what mostly happened was that one person would subconsciously 'select' the first letter. Then, per the quote above about how people would start to guess the final word, more and more people in the group would also start looking at the subsequent letters as the word was spelled out. The researchers found that they were still able to predict the word that was spelled out just by looking at the eye tracking data. Somewhat related experiments have looked at blindfolded participants. As you might have guessed, when the participants couldn't see the board, the resulting answers were far less informative. Here's a short video of an informal demonstration along these lines: I used a Ouija board once many years ago with one of my best friends growing up. And I can attest to the fact that it does feel very convincing, with the planchette moving about without any conscious control. But just because it's not under conscious control doesn't mean it's anything supernatural. It's our subconscious minds that drive the motion.

I totally believe the evolution theory because it has tons of scientific evidence, but I don't get it how marine life evolved to have lungs, limbs, developed, and somehow intelligent brain to live on land? I think part of the problem is people only think about a stereotypical, generic fish, and don't know about or don't think about the wide variety we see in living fish. You mentioned lungs and limbs, so let's take a look at those. And let's start with the limbs, since it makes for cooler videos. First, here's a frogfish. To be clear, frogfish aren't particularly closely related to the first tetrapods. They're adapted to a fully aquatic lifestyle without ever venturing onto land. But yet, they walk underwater, because it's a better way for them to get around, and especially to use their fins to sit on the ocean floor waiting to ambush prey. And here's a type of walking shark. Again, these are fully aquatic sharks. Their walking isn't some type of planning ahead for a life on the land, but a very useful means of locomotion to prowl around a reef. Next, let's move on to lungs. Air breathing is in fact quite common in many lineages of fish. Oxygen is much more consistent in the atmosphere than in the water, so many fish will surface to swallow gulps of air. Somewhere around 400 million years ago, the common ancestor of bony fish evolved a primitive lung as an outgrowth of the stomach as a way to improve oxygen absorption from these swallowed gulps. Over time, some lineages developed more advanced lungs, while others actually went in a different direction, and the lung evolved into a swim bladder. It just so happens that the lineage that evolved a swim bladder has gone on to become the most successful lineage of fish, so it somewhat biases our perception of what's normal. But a look at the bony fish family tree shows lungs to be rather widespread: ABOVE: The lineages in solid black still have lungs, while the lineages with the dashed outlines evolved swim bladders. SOURCE: How did fish evolve the ability to breathe on land? But even in the lineages that traded lungs for swim bladders, in certain environments, it's still beneficial for fish to be able to breathe air, and so various lineages have evolved new adaptations to allow this. Some fish, like bettas, are so dependent on atmospheric oxygen that they'll 'drown' if they can't get to the surface to take a breath. ABOVE SOURCE: Accessory Respiratory Organs of Fishes (With Diagram) | Chordata | Zoology So, just looking at living species of fish, walking and breathing air are relatively common. And from there, it's not a big step (get it?) to begin spending some time on land. Even that is common enough in living fish, from mudskippers to walking catfish to another species of walking shark that I didn't show here (Epaulette Shark Walks on Land). And once you have fish spending some time on land, well, it's not hard to see how they could become even more specialized to spend even more time on land. In other words, there's no need to ponder any special or unique conditions for why our ancestors would have evolved legs or lungs to make the transition from water to land, since we see plenty of analogs in fish alive right now. They’re simply useful features for some fish to have.
