Why did Tim Walz put female tampons and pads in the boys washroom? I have to say, this is one of the stranger tempests in a teapot I've seen in a while. The reality seems like such a mundane law (albeit very beneficial) that I’m surprised it’s managed to draw this much attention. But while most of the manufactured controversy came out of the right-wing, some left-wing responses have also been a bit more rationalization after the fact rather than what the law originally intended, and based more around conjecture than what's actually going on in Minnesota (i.e. it didn't have anything to do with logistics). So first – the civics lessons. Tim Walz didn't write this law. He didn't campaign on it or provide a draft for the legislature to act on. The law was originally sponsored by Sandra Feist in the Minnesota House, in a standalone bill, HF 44 , and then got included in the much larger Education Finance Bill, HF 2497. After going through the full process in the Minnesota House and Senate, the Education Finance Bill was eventually approved by majorities in both chambers, and so Tim Walz signed it into law. But this whole initiative of providing menstrual products to student was never something that Walz himself led. The main purpose of the law originally proposed by Feist is to provide menstrual products to students. This isn't some revolutionary idea new to Minnesota. There are similar laws on the books in 28 states and D.C. to address what some describe as "period poverty". According to Period Products in Schools, 1 in 4 students struggle to afford such products. And one study of a program in NYC found a 2.4% increase in attendance when free period products were offered to students. As one of the students who testified in the Minnesota House during a hearing on the legislation put it, "We cannot learn while we are leaking" (source: Minnesota may soon OK free menstrual products in schools. These teens led the way). ABOVE SOURCE: Period Products in Schools - Alliance for Period Supplies If you want to read the law for yourself, go to the full text of HF2497. It's easy to find the relevant portions. Just do a search for 'menstrual'. Here's the main portion: ARTICLE 1 GENERAL EDUCATION Section 1. [121A.212] ACCESS TO MENSTRUAL PRODUCTS. A school district or charter school must provide students with access to menstrual products at no charge. The products must be available to all menstruating students in restrooms regularly used by students in grades 4 to 12 according to a plan developed by the school district. For purposes of this section, "menstrual products" means pads, tampons, or other similar products used in connection with the menstrual cycle. There's another passage specifying that the budget for this will be "$2 times the adjusted pupil units of the school district for the school year", and another passage including these menstrual products in a list of allowed purposes for "Total operating capital revenue". Note that there's no mandate that tampons have to be supplied in the boys restroom. However, the language was gender neutral, allowing for discretion at the local levels for schools to implement this law. And that gender neutral language was on purpose. According to Feist, the sponsor of the original bill: While the vast majority of the period products will be used in the girls’ bathrooms, the decision was made to structure the bill as gender-inclusive in order to ensure that trans and nonbinary students who menstruate would have equal access to the products they need. SOURCE: Yes, Tim Walz signed a law requiring Minnesota public schools to provide free tampons in school bathrooms Also, as noted in the article, Why Republicans are calling Walz 'Tampon Tim' — and why Democrats embrace it, there was opposition to this gender inclusivity when "Some Minnesota Republicans initially tried to limit the initiative to female-assigned and gender-neutral bathrooms, but were unsuccessful." However, it's interesting to note that the Republican who proposed that amendment did go on to support the final bill, as he felt the overall issue was important, and not worth killing over that compromise. It’s also worth pointing out that schools are free to come up with their own plans to implement the law. According to an editorial from the Minnesota based Star Tribune, A reality check on the ‘Tampon Tim’ meme: At Anoka-Hennepin, the state’s largest school district, the free products are not found in traditional male-only bathrooms, a spokesman said. But they are provided for free to all in “nongendered bathrooms,” girls’ bathrooms or from health staffers. I can't say that absolutely no schools in Minnesota have provided tampons in the boys room, but if the largest school district in the state isn't doing so, it's obviously not a requirement of the law, so long as transgender students can still receive menstrual products if they need them. So basically, Tim Walz signed a large law that had a bunch of different sections dealing with multiple aspects of education funding. Among these was a requirement to provide tampons to students for free, which seems utterly reasonable to me. The language was made specifically gender neutral, allowing individual schools to implement the law as they saw fit, so long as they were still complying and supporting all students who needed menstrual products, which also seems pretty reasonable to me. And just to be clear, the law doesn't actually force schools to provide tampons in the boys room, and as proven in practice, at least one school district cited in the news hasn't.

Do atheists believe that cucumbers could evolve into kangaroos if given enough time? Well, I'm not going to say it's flat out impossible, but it does seem very, very unlikely. This is a great example of how historical contingency constrains evolution, since that's not at all the way us animals evolved in the first place. Here's an evolutionary tree of eukaryotes, which is the group that includes both us and plants. Land plants, which includes cucumbers, are in the top left, while us animals (metazoans) are in the bottom left: ABOVE SOURCE: https://bsapubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.3732/ajb.1300314 This figure also shows multicellularity vs. unicellularity vs. colonial species. Based on the pattern, it appears that multicellularity evolved independently in several lineages. Or in other words, our common ancestor with plants was still unicellular, and that we and plants each took a different path to arrive at multicellularity. The lineage that led to plants had already developed photosynthesis before evolving multicellularity, so all of their development towards multicellularity was geared around that lifestyle. Likewise, our single celled ancestors were already consuming other organisms, so all of our development towards multicellularity was geared around that lifestyle. And at this point in the present, our different lineages are specialized for our respective lifestyles. What's more, they're not particularly compatible lifestyles. While sunlight is very plentiful, it's not particularly energy dense compared to eating other organisms. So, plants get by on a lot less energy than us animals, which is part of the reason they tend to be generally immobile (though you do get occasional fast responses like Venus fly traps). By contrast, when we eat a plant, we're basically getting all that energy the plant has stored up over time in just a few bites, before going on to the next plant and the next plant, so we can spend much more energy on things like moving around (not that animals have to move around, as evidenced by sponges). For something like a cucumber to evolve into something like a kangaroo is a drastic, drastic change in how those organisms make a living. Sure, if I get creative enough, I can think of kinda sorta plausible scenarios where it could happen, but truth be told, they don't actually seem genuinely plausible. What's more, as long as existing animals are around, you've got to worry about the competitive exclusion principle. What incipient animal-like plant would be able to outcompete existing actual animals? So yeah, given enough time, I'm not sure you could completely rule out something like this, but it does seem rather unlikely.

Why are non-professional cyclists drawn to road bikes? Back when I was in college, I bought a somewhat decent mountain bike* to get around. I didn't give a whole lot of thought to mountain bike vs. road bike at the time. I mean, mountain bikes just sounded cooler, and it seemed that a mountain bike would be more robust to the abuse of daily riding, jumping curbs, hitting potholes, and the like. It was fine, got me to and from campus, and I even took it on a nearby trail a handful of times. Riding a bike daily like that for over 2 years got me pretty accustomed to cycling. Fast forward a few years to living in Wichita Falls, Texas, and we have a huge cycling event known as the Hotter'n Hell Hundred, so named for a 100 mile route in potentially 100°F weather (though it now takes place in the morning and so isn't usually quite that hot). A group of us decided to participate one year just to say we did it, but sticking with a shorter 25 mile route. One friend was really into cycling, so he offered to go down to a place in Dallas to pick up good road bike rentals for the weekend – bikes up in the several thousand dollar range if we were going to buy them. ABOVE: The Mass Start at the Hotter'n Hell Hundred SOURCE: 40th Hotter 'N Hell Hundred event photos When I first got up on that road bike and pressed down on the pedal... Wow! The bike just glided across the pavement like it was nothing. And when I stopped pedaling, the bike didn't stop. It just kept on coasting and coasting seemingly forever. There was just no comparison between that road bike and the mountain bike that I'd ridden back in college. The road bike was supremely optimized to be low friction for riding on pavement. Now, I'm still not sure a road bike would have been the best option for me in college with the amount I abused my bike. And there's no way I would have been able to shell out several thousands of dollars for a road bike comparable to that one I rented. But after riding a good road bike when all I was used to before was a mountain bike, I can definitely understand why people opt for road bikes. I mean, it’s in the name. That’s what they’re designed for. *My bike in college was a Raleigh M50 - looked just like this: 2000 Raleigh M50 Front Suspension Mountain Bike for Sale in Mechanicsburg, PA - OfferUp. If memory serves, it cost somewhere around $300 back in the 90s, which would be the equivalent of around $600 today. So not a world class bike, but definitely better than what you find in a typical Walmart.

Is the platypus related to dinosaurs or birds in terms of evolution? All life is related through common descent. So the only question is, how closely? And that's going to depend on your perspective. So sure, in comparison to a rose bush, mammals (including platypuses) and dinosaurs are pretty closely related. If you want to look at the similarities between mammals and dinosaurs, we're both eukaryotes, then animals, then vertebrates, and then tetrapods. So we're more closely related than any organism outside of those groups. But if you're wondering if platypuses are more closely related to dinosaurs than to us, then no. Platypuses are definitely mammals. They have fur, mammary glands, and a host of other features firmly placing them as mammals. However, the lineage that eventually gave rise to platypuses did split off from our lineage a long time ago, before our lineage had developed several other features that we now think of as typically mammalian, such as more developed teats and live birth. So although platypuses have evolved in their own way since the split, they've retained the ancestral condition on things like laying eggs and having a cloaca. Now, there is one other feature of platypuses that sometimes confuses people in that their snout bears a superficial resemblance to a beak, or to a duck's bill. But that really is only superficial. If you compare the skulls, you can see that the underlying structure is not at all similar. A duck's jaw is basically the same shape as the beak, with just a thin coating of keratin on top of the bone (keratin is the same substance as our fingernails). A platypus jaw is very different, and the bone is covered in soft tissue and skin to give it its characteristic shape. The snout is also covered in thousands of electroreceptors it uses to find prey underwater. And as one last note, while baby platypuses are born with teeth, those fall out by adulthood. What looks like possible molars on the skull below are actually bony plates, not teeth. ABOVE: Duck skull on left vs. platypus skull on right - there’s not really any mistaking the two SOURCES: Amazon and Skulls Unlimited, combined by me Anyway, if you want to know how closely related any two different organisms are, a great website is: You can type any two species that are within its database, and it will give an estimate (based on published research) on how long ago their last common ancestor lived. So, for platypuses and us humans, it gives an estimate of 180 million years ago. For platypuses and blue jays (to pick a dinosaur at random), it gives an estimate of 319 million years ago. (And just to be clear, since platypuses are mammals just like us, our last common ancestor with blue jays was also 319 million years ago.) And since I mentioned it up in the beginning, the last common ancestor between all of us animals and a rose bush was around 1.53 billion years ago. So, even though our last common ancestor with a platypus was a long time ago, the last common ancestor with dinosaurs was even longer ago than that, and that last common ancestor with a rose bush was much, much longer ago than even that. What are the units of Einstein’s mass energy equivalence equation E=mc^2? If E were in Joules what would m be? If m were in ng what would E be? Or is there some weird mathematical black magic that makes the units completely unrelatable to normies? Metric only has 7 fundamental units that get defined relative to some standard. Every other unit is derived from these seven: Really, we could use just those 7 units for everything and not have any other units. For example, we define speed as m/s without giving it a special unit. But for simple convenience, we have defined additional units based on those fundamental units, and then given them their own name for shorthand. Relevant to this question, Joules are defined as: J = kg·m²/s² Because there are many of these derived units, you can do conversions between them. Force, for example, gets the derived unit of Newtons, which are defined as follows (which is easy to remember as long as you remember F=ma): N = kg·m/s² And if you look back to the definition of Joules, it should be obvious that you can swap out kg·m/s² for N and get: J = kg·m²/s² J = (kg·m/s²)·m J = N·m It's still the equivalent to kg·m²/s² and still means the same thing. It's just a slightly shorter way to write it. Anyway, looking to Einstein's famous equation: E=mC² E=kg·(m/s)² E=kg·m²/s² E=J So, all the units work out just fine, no black magic required. And for what it's worth, since I'm an engineer in the U.S. and industry standard here is the US Customary System, the equation works just fine with those units, as well. Keeping in mind that a pound force is defined as slug·ft/s² (using the same F=ma), and that the typical unit of energy in USCS is ft·lb, you can run through the units with Einstein's equation: E=mC² E=slug·(ft/s)² E=slug·ft²/s² E=ft·(slug·ft/s²) E=ft·lb Such unit systems are known as 'consistent' systems, where you can go through all this math with the units and have things work out properly. Metric and the foot–pound–second subset of USCS obviously work fine. But there are other consistent systems out there, such as the centimetre–gram–second system or the inch-slinch-second system. For USCS, there's a whole panoply of non-consistent units that require conversion before you start on the real math (like converting BTUs to ft·lb). For metric, you mostly only have to worry about time, making sure everything's done in seconds and not minutes or hours (e.g. km/h is not an official SI unit, neither is Wh for energy). But as long as you do stick with consistent units, all your math in science and engineering will work out just fine.

If you die, is there anything you can do to leave lasting evidence that you have left traces and existed on the earth forever? This reminds me of my favorite poem we learned in my high school lit class: I met a traveller from an antique land, Who said—“Two vast and trunkless legs of stone Stand in the desert. . . . Near them, on the sand, Half sunk a shattered visage lies, whose frown, And wrinkled lip, and sneer of cold command, Tell that its sculptor well those passions read Which yet survive, stamped on these lifeless things, The hand that mocked them, and the heart that fed; And on the pedestal, these words appear: My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings; Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair! Nothing beside remains. Round the decay Of that colossal Wreck, boundless and bare The lone and level sands stretch far away. —Percy Shelley, "Ozymandias" To spell it out, no. Nothing you do will last forever. In time, we will all eventually be forgotten. It’s vanity and hubris to expect anything different. Don’t be Ozymandias. Why do atheists put gods from polytheistic religions alongside the Abrahamic one as if they're equal? Polytheism is impossible because separate realities or existences are impossible. There can only be one god. To be honest, polytheism seems (slightly) more plausible than monotheism, especially if you're thinking of an all-knowing, all-powerful, and benevolent God. It comes down to the problem of evil*. The amount of suffering in the world just isn't consistent with this type of good monotheistic God. But with polytheism, especially when you allow for all the different gods to have different personalities and different motivations, with none of them actually having full control over the world, then the problem of evil isn't really a problem, anymore. It's just a consequence of the competition and conflicts between all these imperfect gods, and humans getting the short end of the stick. Of course, the other obvious solution to the problem of evil from a monotheist perspective is to drop the benevolent part. If God was evil, well, you would expect a world full of suffering. *I know apologists like to bring up free will or other excuses, but these are never very convincing given much thought. What is the reasoning behind atheists thinking it's illogical to believe in god? Should people be allowed to have their own beliefs without being challenged by others? Let's take your latter two questions first: Should people be allowed to have their own beliefs... Yes without being challenged by others? Absolutely not. This is the type of delicate little snowflake mentality that so many people complain about. All beliefs should be robust enough that they can withstand inspection. If they're not, then maybe they weren't such good beliefs in the first place. Now, I'm not saying life needs to be one continuous debate during all waking hours. There's a time and place for everything, and there's a difference between debate and badgering (or to make a verb of a different animal, sea lioning). But yes, you should at least occasionally have discussions with people who disagree with you about challenging topics – politics, religion, morality, pineapple on pizza, etc. If you never challenge yourself, you'll never grow. And if you limit yourself to echo chambers of only like minded people, you'll never truly understand the wider world and why different people do things differently from you. I can think of plenty of examples from my own life where I'm grateful to the people who challenged me and helped me to see things differently. As far as your first question, well, that could be an entire book. But the short of it is, all the evidence we do have for God and Christianity is best explained as a mythology that developed out of previous mythologies. Heck, we even have evidence of Yahweh's origins in the Canaanite pantheon as a storm god – NOT the one and only God and creator of the universe. Other religions and their holy books are largely similar in that they've developed over generations as mythology. And the other big, glaring problem that they all have is a complete lack of credible evidence. Oh sure, Hindus, Buddhists, Christians, and Muslims all get warm fuzzy feelings when they pray, and some even manage to convince themselves that unlikely events and coincidences are evidence of their particular god(s) (but obviously, not the other gods). But this evidence hardly ever seems credible to outsiders who don't already share their beliefs. So there you go. We think it's not reasonable to believe in gods in general because there's no good evidence, and the capital G God in particular because the evidence we do have shows that he's a product of human myth making. And while we all certainly have a right to hold any beliefs we want, we should also be open to being challenged about those beliefs. That's the only way we grow as individuals.

Is a ruler exactly 12 inches? Surely if you zoom in trillions and trillions and trillions of times, then the length of the ruler has to be ever so slightly different than exactly 12 inches, correct? This brings up a topic that I found enormously fascinating when I first became an engineer, and that I think is drastically underappreciated by the general public – tolerances. This is such a huge topic that I could write an entire book about it, because people have, in fact, written entire books about it. ABOVE: 367 pages worth of explanation about tolerancing SOURCE: Amazon The issue, like you've correctly surmised, is that it's essentially impossible to make an object exactly a certain dimension. And in truth, you don't usually need it to be that exact, anyway. So, when I make a technical drawing to send to a machine shop to get a part made, I don't just call out the dimensions of all the features. I also call out how close the actual measurements of the finished part need to be to those dimensions on the drawing. A typical title block on a drawing might look something like this, with standard tolerances based on how many decimal points you use in a dimension: So, if I call out a length as 3.0, that gets a tolerance of ±0.03", so the machine shop could make that feature anything from 2.97" to 3.03", and it would be acceptable. If it was something that needed to be very precise, then I might call out the dimension as 3.0000, in which case the machine shop would have to make the feature to within ±0.001", or 2.999" to 3.001". Sometimes, those default tolerances aren't enough. It might be something like a hole that would work out okay if it was a little too big, but not too small, so you might specify an asymmetrical tolerance, like +.01/-0. Or, it might be something like a bearing housing that needs to be even tighter than 0.001". In those cases, you'll specify the tolerance right at the dimension on the drawing, rather than rely on the default dimensions from the title block. There are all types of things that can be covered in tolerancing – lengths, circularity, flatness, concentricity, perpendicularity, etc. We don't always take the time to mark such figures like we should, sometimes relying on implied understandings and quality workmanship, but that can also get you into trouble. I remember one specialized nut we designed that had to fit inside another hole without a whole lot of clearance. The nut was threaded on the inside and round on the outside, with a couple flats carved on the top to fit a wrench. We just assumed that the part would get made on a lathe and that the features would all be concentric, so we didn't think to specify a concentricity tolerance. Well, however the machine shop made it, the center bore of the nut with the threads wasn't concentric with the outer diameter, so it didn't fit into that hole it needed to fit into. But since we didn't specify a concentricity tolerance, we had no grounds to reject the part. We just had to eat the cost, redo the drawing, and pay them to make another one. Measuring parts is another whole artform unto itself. We have instruments that are capable of high precision measurements, such as micrometers, dial calipers, and even (shudder) Vernier calipers. But when you're measuring things on the order of a few thousandths of an inch, it doesn't take too much force on the instrument to deform the part or the instrument itself to give a false reading. I'm somewhat handy at getting reasonable measurements with my dial caliper, but I always left the real measurements to the machinists and QA inspectors – I trusted them a whole lot more. ABOVE: A dial caliper with .001" graduations – it would be easy to push too hard and get that to read 0.712″ instead of the 0.710″ it currently shows SOURCE: https://instrumentation.com/120a-6-dial-caliper-hardened-stainless-steel-0-6-range-001-graduations.aspx Getting back to your original question, the tolerance on a typical 12" ruler that you'd buy from Walmart usually won't be just super tight. The smallest divisions on the ruler are liable to only be 1/16" of inch to begin with, or 0.0625". If that's the smallest mark on the ruler, nobody's going to notice if it's off by a few thousandths of an inch. So the tolerance for making such rulers can be a bit on the loose side. I didn't even get into Geometric dimensioning and tolerancing, which is another entire topic. It expands on the basic level of tolerancing I already described in this answer. It's a bit more complicated than traditional tolerancing, but ideally gives more wiggle room to the manufacturers by understanding the intent behind the tolerances.

What is the belief of atheists regarding the value of all life, including unborn fetuses? Now that is a huge philosophical question right there. All life covers a gigantic range of life forms, everything from bacteria to insects to oak trees to house cats to people. And however people might wax poetic about the value of life, the pragmatic lesson from our actions is that we don't value all life the same. We buy cleaners and disinfectants that proudly advertise how effective they are at killing life forms. We have no qualms using insecticides on our crops, or setting traps or poison around our houses to keep rodents or other pests from destroying our possessions. We kill all types of animals so that we can eat them. Even vegans and vegetarians kill countless plants for food. So on a general level, merely being 'alive' is not enough to automatically earn something any particularly high 'value' or protection from human actions. We, each and every one of us personally, kill untold numbers of life forms on a daily basis. ABOVE: This cleaner is advertising a virtual 'genocide' on a microscopic level SOURCE: Uline So how do we value some lives more than others? What makes it wrong to kill an organism? As a short, simple thought experiment, just imagine if we ever did discover intelligent alien life. I'm nearly certain we would extend some types of rights or values to this life. But keep in mind that such aliens would be completely, well, alien. They wouldn't be human beings. They wouldn't be closely related to human beings. They wouldn't have genetics similar to human beings. Heck, their biochemistry might not even use DNA as the genetic molecule. So any arguments of value based on any of those things are, at best, incomplete, and at worst, not really the basis in the first place. It seems that the way we value life is some combination of intelligence and sentience, along with less objective emotional reasons. Dolphins, for example, seem to be very intelligent creatures, with rich emotional lives and social connections. So, many of us feel that killing a dolphin for no good reason is wrong. The bacteria on my kitchen counter, on the other hand, seem very unlikely to have any sentience. So, we don't bat an eye when we wipe down our counters with powerful disinfectants that kill millions of bacteria in one fell swoop. And then there are tradeoffs based on how those other lives affect us. For my own part, for example, I generally don't kill any bugs I find in my house, not even the stinging or biting ones like wasps or spiders. I'll either just let them be, or catch them in a glass and release them outside. But when I found termites getting into the framing around my garage door? You can bet I sprayed it all down myself, then called in an exterminator to treat the entire perimeter of my house. As soon as those termites crossed the line into damaging my property, I wasn't nearly so tolerant. As far as fetuses, and assuming you mean human fetuses as opposed to other mammals (which isn't really at all certain in a discussion on all life, so forgive me if I went too far in my assumption), it still depends on what you mean by 'value'? People can value inanimate objects, after all, so it's certainly possible for people to value a fetus simply because. And many would-be parents will certainly value a fetus for the potential it offers, to eventually develop into an actual person. But if you're asking if we as a society need to extend the same types of rights and protections to a fetus as to an actual person, I would return to my prior points, particularly sentience. This is the same type of consideration we use for end of life decisions, saying that it is okay to cease life support when it's clear that a person is brain dead. And it seems a fitting consideration for start of life decisions, and when a fetus transitions from a mere conglomeration of unconscious cells to an actual person capable of experience. So when does this transition happen? Here's an article that addresses this question: To quote the article: Consciousness requires a sophisticated network of highly interconnected components, nerve cells. Its physical substrate, the thalamo-cortical complex that provides consciousness with its highly elaborate content, begins to be in place between the 24th and 28th week of gestation. Roughly two months later synchrony of the electroencephalographic (EEG) rhythm across both cortical hemispheres signals the onset of global neuronal integration. Thus, many of the circuit elements necessary for consciousness are in place by the third trimester. So while the 'hardware' for experience is in place around the start of the third trimester, if you're looking to synchrony of the EEG rhythm to indicate consciousness, that doesn't occur until a couple months after that, well into the third trimester. So it would seem that throughout most of its development, even though a human fetus is alive in the sense of biological activity and metabolism, it lacks the sentience that would grant it larger considerations of human rights. Anyway, this answer of mine barely scratches the surface. There are other measures of value besides the value of the individual life form, such as biodiversity and the health of ecosystems. There are plenty of other philosophical considerations and moral frameworks, such as social contract theory, utilitarianism, virtue ethics, etc. And of course, my answer is only my own – I can't pretend to speak for all atheists. But hopefully this gives some small sense of the considerations that go into this issue.

According to Newton's 2nd law, F=ma, but when we push the wall, why does it not accelerate? Well, the more typical way we saw that equation in my engineering classes* was: ΣF = ma Don't let the Σ scare you. It just means the summation, or that you add all the forces together. You typically do this with what are known as free body diagrams, where you depict all the various forces on an object. Here, for example, is a simple beam: SOURCE: How to Draw Free Body Diagrams with examples | DegreeTutors.com Two forces are being applied to the beam at different locations, one force of 45 kN (10,116 lbs), the other force of 30 kN (6744 lbs). But you know the beam is being supported at each end, so you know those supports are going to push back. I won't go through the math here, but it's a pretty basic statics problem to figure out what they are: SOURCE: How to Draw Free Body Diagrams with examples | DegreeTutors.com So, returning to ΣF = ma, let's just double check what all the forces add up to, keeping in mind the directions the forces are being applied: ΣF = 48 kN + (-45 kN) + (-30 kN) + 27 kN ΣF = 0 So, if ΣF = 0, then it also follows that a = 0. No acceleration. Newtons' Law still holds. And of course, for your particular question, when you push on a wall, it’s almost always attached to something, so there will be a reaction force pushing back, keeping the forces balanced. Once again, ΣF = 0, so no acceleration *Once you get out of school, people get a bit lazier about always including the Σ, since all engineers know that it’s implied.
